questions.topic: Device malfunction follow-up and procedural decisions
questions.question: A pacemaker generator has eroded through the skin, with a small draining sinus. The patient is afebrile, blood cultures are negative and echocardiography shows no vegetation. Extraction risk is acceptable. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Arrange complete system removal with appropriate antimicrobial treatment and reassessment of pacing needs
Treat with antibiotics while retaining the system because blood cultures are negative
Remove the generator and retain the transvenous leads because no vegetation is seen
Revise the pocket and close the skin after local debridement
questions.explanation:
Pacemaker Pocket Erosion and Definite Device Infection

Correct answer: Arrange complete system removal with appropriate antimicrobial treatment and reassessment of pacing needs

Exposed Hardware Establishes the Diagnosis

**Generator erosion, a pocket sinus or purulent drainage constitutes definite pocket infection.** Absence of fever, bacteremia or an echocardiographic vegetation does not exclude this localized form of CIED infection.

Differentiate a superficial early incisional infection confined to skin and subcutaneous tissue without pocket communication. That limited condition can sometimes be treated without extraction; the distinction cannot be extended to exposed generator hardware.

Obtain appropriate blood cultures before antibiotics when clinically feasible, assess systemic involvement and involve an experienced extraction and infection team. Do not postpone necessary antimicrobial treatment in a septic patient.

Source Control and Subsequent Pacing

**Definite CIED infection generally requires complete hardware removal plus antimicrobial treatment.** Biofilm on retained components makes antibiotics or local revision alone prone to failure.

Tailor antimicrobial choice and duration to cultures, pocket-only versus systemic disease, valve involvement and extraction findings. An uncomplicated isolated pocket infection after removal commonly receives 10–14 days of treatment; endocarditis requires a longer organism-specific course.

Reassess whether pacing remains indicated and provide a safe temporary strategy if the patient is dependent. Reimplant at a different appropriate site or use another suitable platform only after infection control and the relevant culture-clearance criteria are met. Leadless pacing can reduce pocket concerns but does not replace source control. If extraction risk is prohibitive, specialist suppressive approaches are exceptions requiring explicit individualized assessment, not equivalent curative alternatives for the patient described.

Treat with antibiotics while retaining the system because blood cultures are negative: Antibiotics with retained hardware may be used in exceptional patients who cannot undergo extraction, but exposed hardware establishes contamination and definite pocket infection. Negative blood cultures do not make retention the standard curative approach.

Remove the generator and retain the transvenous leads because no vegetation is seen: A vegetation need not be visible for the system to be infected. Retained leads can sustain biofilm and relapse, so isolated generator removal is inadequate for definite pocket infection when complete removal is feasible.

Revise the pocket and close the skin after local debridement: Pocket revision may address selected noninfectious mechanical problems before exposure. Established erosion with a draining sinus represents infection, and closure over retained contaminated hardware does not provide reliable source control.

EHRA international consensus on CIED infection, 2020 — https://doi.org/10.1093/europace/euz246

HRS multisociety lead management and extraction consensus update, 2026 — https://www.heartrhythmjournal.com/article/S1547-5271%2826%2902264-2/abstract

questions.question: An adult has several weeks of fever, hematuria with red-cell casts, low complement and a splenic wedge-shaped infarct. Two separately collected blood-culture sets grow Streptococcus mitis. No murmur is heard. Which diagnosis best unifies the findings?
options: Left-sided infective endocarditis
ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis
Lupus-associated Libman–Sacks endocarditis
Malignancy-associated nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis
questions.explanation:
Endocarditis Without a Detectable Murmur

Correct answer: Left-sided infective endocarditis

Recognize More Than a Valve Auscultation Diagnosis

**IE can present through systemic infection, embolization and immune-mediated injury before a clear murmur is detected.** The absence of a murmur cannot exclude an infected endocardial surface.

A left-sided vegetation can embolize to spleen, kidney, brain or other systemic territories. A splenic infarct can be initially sterile but may later become infected; persistent focal pain or fever warrants reassessment.

Glomerulonephritis can produce hematuria, casts and complement consumption. It differs from a renal arterial embolus, although more than one renal mechanism can coexist in the same patient.

Establish the Endocardial and Microbiological Evidence

**Concordant S. mitis cultures in this phenotype make IE an urgent diagnostic priority.** Obtain cardiac imaging and integrate the results with a named diagnostic framework rather than declaring a valve lesion from bacteremia alone.

TTE is usually the first cardiac study; TEE is needed when suspicion persists, anatomy is prosthetic or the initial study does not adequately define disease. Assess regurgitation, ventricular function and local extension as well as vegetation size.

Review the oral and other potential portals of entry, existing valve disease, prior procedures and intracardiac material. Do not begin an immune-treatment pathway for presumed primary vasculitis without addressing the infection evidence. Once cultures and susceptibility are available, provide appropriate pathogen-directed antibiotics and assess HF, uncontrolled infection and embolic indications for surgery. The clinical lesson is to connect the systemic findings to a possible infected endovascular source while confirming its location and extent, rather than requiring a classic murmur or assuming that every renal abnormality is primary autoimmune disease.

ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis: Vasculitis can cause fever and glomerular injury, but the concordant typical-organism bacteremia and embolic lesion make an endovascular infection a more coherent explanation. Infection can also generate misleading immune-test abnormalities.

Lupus-associated Libman–Sacks endocarditis: Sterile valve lesions can occur with lupus and accompany nephritis or emboli. The repeated typical-organism cultures instead require active investigation for infectious endocarditis rather than assuming a sterile immune process.

Malignancy-associated nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis: NBTE can cause systemic emboli and may occur without a prominent murmur. It does not best explain repeated oral-streptococcal bacteremia with an inflammatory renal syndrome; malignancy and infection are not distinguished by the murmur alone.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

Duke–ISCVID diagnostic criteria, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciad271

questions.question: A stable antibiotic-naive adult has a subacute illness strongly suspicious for IE, without shock or another need for immediate resuscitation. Which collection plan best follows ESC 2023 practice?
options: Obtain the sets only when the temperature next reaches its peak
Obtain one peripheral set and begin treatment once it flags positive
Obtain three adequately filled peripheral culture sets before starting antibiotics
Begin empirical antibiotics and collect three sets after the first dose
questions.explanation:
Pre-Antibiotic Blood Cultures in a Stable Suspected Case

Correct answer: Obtain three adequately filled peripheral culture sets before starting antibiotics

Collect Enough Blood Before Suppressing the Organism

**Blood-culture yield depends importantly on adequate volume and obtaining samples before antibiotics.** A culture set ordinarily contains an aerobic and an anaerobic bottle.

ESC 2023 recommends at least three sets at roughly thirty-minute intervals in the appropriate stable suspected case. Use meticulous asepsis and appropriate peripheral sampling; adult bottles commonly require about ==8–10 mL== each according to the system.

Document collection times, sites and previous antimicrobial exposure. A central-line specimen can be informative for a line-source question but should not simply replace appropriate peripheral cultures for suspected IE.

Separate Collection Practice From Diagnostic Classification

**The recommended sampling strategy is not identical to a rule for counting major criteria.** Duke–ISCVID 2023 removed older complex timing and separate-venipuncture requirements from its formal culture criterion.

Typical organisms in at least two separate culture sets can satisfy its microbiological major criterion. That does not mean only two bottles are sufficient, nor that a stable patient should skip recommended diagnostic sampling.

In IE, continuous bacteremia means there is no need to wait for a fever peak. Inform the laboratory when unusual organisms, previous antibiotics or a culture-negative process are concerns. Repeated recovery of the same organism must be interpreted with the organism’s IE association, prosthetic material and clinical findings. An isolated skin organism requires contextual review rather than automatic dismissal or automatic diagnosis. If the patient deteriorates, collect promptly and begin appropriate treatment; the stable sampling timetable must not become a delay rule in shock.

Obtain the sets only when the temperature next reaches its peak: Timing at a fever peak is useful for some historical sampling assumptions, but IE commonly produces continuous bacteremia. Waiting for a spike can delay useful specimens without improving the diagnostic strategy.

Obtain one peripheral set and begin treatment once it flags positive: One set can detect bacteremia, but provides less sensitivity and less ability to distinguish contamination from sustained infection. The stable suspected-IE presentation permits an adequate pre-treatment collection rather than relying on a single specimen.

Begin empirical antibiotics and collect three sets after the first dose: Treatment before collection can be necessary when delay would compromise an unstable patient. The supplied stable untreated presentation allows cultures first and avoids preventable antibiotic-suppressed culture-negative disease.

Duke–ISCVID diagnostic criteria, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciad271

questions.question: A patient with a prosthetic valve has probable endovascular infection, hypotension, altered mentation and rising lactate. Cultures can be collected immediately, but completing the usual spaced stable-patient collection would postpone antibiotics. Which sequence is most appropriate?
options: Complete the full spaced sampling sequence before administering antibiotics
Collect cultures promptly and start appropriate empirical IV therapy immediately while resuscitating
Obtain TEE confirmation before choosing whether to start antimicrobial treatment
Wait for an initial culture Gram stain before selecting empirical therapy
questions.explanation:
Blood Cultures and Antibiotic Timing in Septic Shock

Correct answer: Collect cultures promptly and start appropriate empirical IV therapy immediately while resuscitating

Preserve Yield Without Sacrificing Time-Critical Treatment

**The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends blood cultures as soon as possible, ideally before antibiotics, and immediate antimicrobial treatment for probable or definite sepsis and for septic shock.** The ideal treatment target is within one hour of recognition.

Collect the feasible adequately filled sets promptly while other staff establish monitoring, access and resuscitation. Do not interpret the stable IE culture-spacing recommendation as a required untreated waiting period in shock.

Record antibiotic timing and sampling details, because subsequent negative cultures may reflect pre-treatment. Inform microbiology of the prosthetic and acquisition context.

Treat the Source and Define the Anatomy in Parallel

**Empirical coverage depends on valve setting, healthcare exposure, previous antibiotics, resistance risk and organ function.** Early prosthetic or healthcare-associated disease requires a different assessment from a stable community-acquired native-valve presentation.

Obtain urgent echocardiographic assessment for valve dysfunction, abscess, dehiscence and other complications. TEE commonly adds essential information around a prosthesis, but treatment does not wait for a completed scan.

Coordinate infectious-disease, cardiac and critical-care teams and involve surgery promptly if HF, uncontrolled infection or another urgent indication is present. Follow perfusion, renal function, lactate trend and subsequent cultures and narrow therapy when reliable susceptibility data permit. Fluids and vasoactive support are individualized to ventricular and valve physiology; they do not replace antimicrobial and anatomical source control. Conversely, giving an antibiotic dose is not the end of the shock response. The correct sequence keeps cultures, stabilization, treatment and diagnostic work moving together rather than finishing every diagnostic step before initiating time-critical care.

Complete the full spaced sampling sequence before administering antibiotics: A spaced collection is appropriate in a stable suspected case. It must not delay time-critical treatment of probable infection with shock; prompt feasible sampling and treatment take priority.

Obtain TEE confirmation before choosing whether to start antimicrobial treatment: TEE is important for locating prosthetic-valve infection and complications. A patient with probable infectious shock requires immediate treatment and stabilization while the imaging pathway proceeds.

Wait for an initial culture Gram stain before selecting empirical therapy: A rapid Gram stain can refine treatment when available, but waiting for culture growth in shock delays effective coverage. Start a context-appropriate empirical regimen and revise it as microbiology becomes available.

questions.question: A patient receiving active treatment for MSSA bacteremia has repeat positive cultures after 72 hours. A technically limited TTE shows no vegetation. The patient has new back pain. Which next plan is most appropriate?
options: Change to vancomycin and reassess imaging after cultures clear
Repeat TTE after a further two weeks of treatment
Investigate endovascular infection with TEE and search for a metastatic or uncontrolled focus
Obtain spinal MRI and manage an isolated vertebral infection
questions.explanation:
Persistent Staphylococcus aureus Bacteremia

Correct answer: Investigate endovascular infection with TEE and search for a metastatic or uncontrolled focus

Treat Persistence as a Signal to Reassess the Entire Episode

**S. aureus bacteremia can reflect endovascular infection and can seed distant structures.** Persistently positive cultures increase concern even when an initial echo appears unrevealing.

Confirm that the agent is active, appropriately dosed and delivered and that susceptibility and identification are reliable. Review vascular access, implanted material and any removable source.

Repeat blood cultures to document clearance rather than substituting a falling inflammatory marker. New focal back pain warrants assessment for vertebral osteomyelitis or an associated collection according to the clinical findings.

questions.question: With no pathological confirmation available, which combination meets the clinical definition of definite infective endocarditis in the 2023 Duke–ISCVID criteria?
options: One major criterion and two minor criteria
One major criterion and three minor criteria
Four minor criteria without a major criterion

questions.explanation:
Clinical Classification With Duke–ISCVID Criteria

Correct answer: One major criterion and three minor criteria

Clinical Definite and Possible Categories

**Duke–ISCVID 2023 retains three routes to clinically definite IE.** These are combinations of qualifying categories, rather than a count of every abnormal test or every positive culture bottle.

A microbiological major criterion and an imaging major criterion can provide two major criteria. Repeated cultures satisfying the same microbiological category do not become multiple major criteria.

Possible IE applies when its minimum combination is met but a definite route is not. Thus one major plus two minor criteria remains possible; four minor criteria without a major also remain possible.

Pathological Evidence and Clinical Judgment

**Definite IE can also be established through qualifying pathological evidence.** Identification of organisms or active endocarditis in specified tissue must be interpreted in the clinical context, including previous treatment and potential contamination.

Clinical criteria include microbiological, imaging and qualifying surgical major domains. Minor domains include predisposition, fever, vascular phenomena, immunological phenomena and specified evidence falling short of major definitions.

Do not withhold necessary therapy while waiting for a patient to acquire enough criteria. Early disease, prosthetic shadowing and previous antibiotics can reduce the evidence available at presentation. Conversely, a classification label does not independently determine the organism, antibiotic regimen, duration or need for surgery. Those decisions require the microbiological and anatomical assessment. Reassess unresolved cases with appropriately repeated cultures, echocardiography and selected additional tests rather than repeatedly counting the same domain. A competing explanation must be actively evaluated when the phenotype or microbiology is inconsistent.

Duke–ISCVID component | Qualifying combination or evidence

Clinical definite | 2 major; or 1 major + 3 minor; or 5 minor

Possible, if not definite | 1 major + 1–2 minor; or 3–4 minor

Microbiological major | Typical organism in ≥2 sets; nontypical organism in ≥3 sets; or specified organism-specific blood molecular/serological evidence

Imaging major | Qualifying echo/CT lesion such as vegetation, abscess or fistula; significant new regurgitation on echo; new prosthetic dehiscence; or qualifying FDG uptake

Surgical major | Direct operative evidence when qualifying imaging and subsequent histological/microbiological confirmation are absent

Minor: predisposition | Qualifying valve disease, prosthetic or repair material, previous IE, CHD, CIED, HOCM or injection drug use

Minor: fever | Documented temperature ==>38°C==

Minor: vascular | Arterial embolus, septic pulmonary infarct, cerebral/splenic abscess, infective aneurysm, intracranial or conjunctival hemorrhage, Janeway lesions or purulent purpura

Minor: immunological | Rheumatoid factor, Osler nodes, Roth spots or qualifying immune-complex glomerulonephritis

Minor: microbiological | Compatible evidence short of major, with the specified contaminant exclusions

Minor: imaging | Qualifying early prosthetic FDG uptake within 3 months

Minor: physical examination | New regurgitant murmur only if echocardiography is unavailable; a changing pre-existing murmur is insufficient

Pathological route | Separate qualifying organism or active-endocarditis tissue evidence in the appropriate clinical context

One major criterion and two minor criteria: This combination reaches possible IE but does not reach the clinical definite threshold. It can still justify urgent investigation and treatment when the overall clinical probability is high.

Four minor criteria without a major criterion: Three or four minor criteria can support possible IE. Five minor criteria are required for the clinical definite route when there is no major criterion.

One major criterion without a minor criterion: A major finding demands clinical evaluation, but a single major criterion alone does not meet the clinical possible or definite combinations. A separate qualifying pathological finding would use a different route.

questions.question: A patient with a prosthetic valve has fever of 38.6°C and Enterococcus faecalis in two separate blood-culture sets. Initial cardiac imaging provides no major imaging finding. No other criteria are present. Which additional finding would establish clinically definite IE under Duke–ISCVID 2023?
options: Newly documented splenomegaly without an embolic lesion
A third culture set growing the same E. faecalis
A further rise in serum C-reactive protein
An imaging-confirmed new splenic arterial embolus
questions.explanation:
Adding a Distinct Criterion Rather Than Recounting Cultures

Correct answer: An imaging-confirmed new splenic arterial embolus

Count the Existing Findings Correctly

**The starting combination is one major and two minor criteria.** The typical-organism cultures provide the microbiological major criterion, the prosthetic valve provides predisposition, and the temperature above ==38°C== provides fever.

E. faecalis is a typical organism in Duke–ISCVID 2023 irrespective of acquisition setting or an identified primary source. The two separate positive sets qualify here; an isolated bottle must not be silently substituted for the stated evidence.

Initial imaging without a qualifying lesion contributes no imaging major criterion. It also does not erase the clinical suspicion or prove that a prosthetic valve is uninfected.

Recognize a New Vascular Domain

**A documented splenic arterial embolus adds a vascular minor criterion.** The resulting one major plus three minor combination reaches clinically definite IE.

Arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts and other specified vascular manifestations belong to one vascular domain. Multiple lesions within that domain should not be counted as separate minor criteria merely because they involve different sites.

Immunological phenomena form a different minor domain and include qualifying immune-complex glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots and rheumatoid factor. Fever measurements on several days still count as one fever domain. Similarly, serial positive cultures can show persistence without multiplying a microbiological major criterion. This distinction protects against overclassification while preserving the clinical importance of each new observation. Continue anatomical assessment and evaluate embolic complications even after a definite classification is reached; the label is a diagnostic framework, not evidence that the extent of infection or its treatment requirements have been fully defined.

Newly documented splenomegaly without an embolic lesion: Splenomegaly can accompany a prolonged infection and deserves investigation. Enlargement alone is not equivalent to a vascular embolus and does not independently fulfill the vascular minor criterion.

A third culture set growing the same E. faecalis: Additional concordant cultures strengthen evidence of sustained bacteremia and guide clearance assessment. The existing typical-organism cultures already satisfy the microbiological major category, so another set does not create a second major criterion.

A further rise in serum C-reactive protein: CRP can support assessment of inflammation and its trajectory during treatment. It is nonspecific and is not an additional Duke–ISCVID minor criterion, so its rise does not supply the missing category.

questions.question: An older adult develops E. faecalis bacteremia after urinary instrumentation. Two separate blood-culture sets are positive. No prosthetic valve is present. Under Duke–ISCVID 2023, how should this microbiology be classified?
options: A major criterion only if intracardiac prosthetic material is present
A microbiological minor criterion because the source is urinary
A major criterion only if a third culture set is positive
A microbiological major criterion despite the apparent urinary source
questions.explanation:
Enterococcus faecalis Bacteremia With a Urinary Source

Correct answer: A microbiological major criterion despite the apparent urinary source

Interpret Typical as an Association With Endocarditis

**Duke–ISCVID 2023 lists E. faecalis as typical independently of acquisition setting or the primary infection source.** A urinary portal can explain entry into blood without proving that a valve has escaped secondary infection.

The stem specifies two separate positive sets, not two positive bottles from one set. The distinction is essential when applying a culture-based threshold.

A set usually comprises an aerobic and an anaerobic bottle collected together. Adequate volume, collection before antibiotics where feasible and careful asepsis remain clinically important even though older classification timing rules were simplified.

Separate a Major Finding From a Complete Diagnosis

**This finding establishes one microbiological major criterion, not clinically definite IE by itself.** Integrate the physical findings, fever, risk factors, embolic or immune features and cardiac imaging.

Do not automatically extrapolate this specific typical-organism designation to all enterococci. Organism identification matters, and a different species may require the nontypical culture rule under the named framework.

Evaluate the urinary obstruction or instrumentation-related source and document bacteremia clearance while assessing whether cardiac imaging is needed. The two investigations can be complementary: source identification is not a substitute for consideration of endovascular seeding. Conversely, not every episode meeting one major criterion requires a full IE treatment course. A defensible final diagnosis requires assessment of the entire episode, including its clinical course and anatomical evidence. Once IE is established, susceptibility, valve setting, renal function and complications guide antimicrobial combinations, duration and the need for source control. These treatment decisions cannot be inferred from the word typical alone.

A major criterion only if intracardiac prosthetic material is present: Intracardiac material expands the list of typical organisms to include selected additional pathogens. E. faecalis is already typical without that context and does not require a prosthesis to meet the culture definition.

A microbiological minor criterion because the source is urinary: A positive culture that falls short of a major definition may contribute a microbiological minor criterion. E. faecalis in the stated number of sets meets the revised typical-organism major definition even when a primary source is identified.

A major criterion only if a third culture set is positive: Three or more separate positive sets are the culture threshold for organisms that only occasionally or rarely cause IE. E. faecalis is in the typical group, for which two separate positive sets suffice.

Duke–ISCVID diagnostic criteria, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciad271

questions.question: In a patient being assessed for culture-negative endocarditis, which blood test is explicitly sufficient for a microbiological major criterion under Duke–ISCVID 2023?
options: A Coxiella phase-II IgG titre of 1:1600 in isolation
A validated blood PCR positive for Tropheryma whipplei
A Bartonella henselae IgG titre of 1:128 in isolation
A single blood-culture bottle growing Staphylococcus epidermidis
questions.explanation:
Blood Molecular Evidence in Culture-Negative Endocarditis

Correct answer: A validated blood PCR positive for Tropheryma whipplei

Use Organism-Specific Tests Rather Than Any Positive Molecular Result

**The 2023 criteria recognize blood nucleic-acid evidence for three specified fastidious pathogens.** This gives selected culture-negative investigations a formal role without treating every positive molecular assay as proof of IE.

The qualifying organisms are C. burnetii, Bartonella species and T. whipplei. PCR and other appropriate nucleic-acid techniques can recover evidence when routine culture is unrevealing.

A positive result is interpreted with assay validity, clinical phenotype and alternative sources of the signal. A major criterion remains one part of a diagnostic framework; it does not replace imaging or the search for complications.

Choose Serology and Tissue Testing Deliberately

**Organism, specimen and method determine how a result is counted.** A blood assay, a valve-tissue result and a nonspecific inflammatory or fungal biomarker are not interchangeable.

Coxiella phase-I and Bartonella IgG serology have specified major thresholds. Use the assay methodology and laboratory interpretation rather than substituting an arbitrary positive-screen threshold.

If operative tissue is available, coordinate culture, histology and targeted or broad-range molecular methods before the specimen is divided or fixed. Prior treatment can reduce culture yield while molecular signals may persist after successful treatment, so an isolated result needs context. Exposure history can guide testing, but the absence of a remembered exposure does not safely exclude these infections. A culture-negative episode after antibiotics may still be due to an ordinary bacterial pathogen; it should not automatically be reclassified as a fastidious infection. Avoid ordering a large unselected panel and equating whichever assay is positive with the cause of a valve lesion.

Qualifying result in Duke–ISCVID 2023 | Major threshold

Blood nucleic-acid test | C. burnetii, Bartonella spp. or T. whipplei

C. burnetii serology | Phase-I IgG ==>1:800==, or equivalent method-specific result

B. henselae or B. quintana serology | IgG ==≥1:800== by the specified immunofluorescence approach, or equivalent result

A Coxiella phase-II IgG titre of 1:1600 in isolation: Phase-II antibodies are useful in evaluating Q fever, particularly acute infection. The specified IE serological major criterion uses phase-I IgG above its threshold; a high isolated phase-II titre cannot be substituted for it.

A Bartonella henselae IgG titre of 1:128 in isolation: Bartonella serology is appropriate in a compatible culture-negative presentation. This result does not reach the specified IgG major threshold of at least 1:800, and lower titres require contextual interpretation and potentially further testing.

A single blood-culture bottle growing Staphylococcus epidermidis: Coagulase-negative staphylococci are important in prosthetic infection, but one isolated positive bottle can also represent contamination. It does not supply the stated repeated-set major evidence, and the organism-specific single-culture exception for Coxiella cannot be applied to it.

questions.question: Six weeks after valve replacement, a patient with suspected PVE has intense focal periprosthetic FDG uptake on a technically adequate study interpreted by an experienced team. How do the published 2023 Duke–ISCVID and ESC diagnostic frameworks treat this finding?
options: Duke–ISCVID counts early uptake as major; ESC restricts it to minor
Both frameworks require waiting three months before the finding can contribute
Both frameworks classify any postoperative FDG uptake as major
Duke–ISCVID counts early uptake as minor; ESC can count the characteristic pattern as major
questions.explanation:
Early Prosthetic-Valve FDG Uptake: Name the Framework

Correct answer: Duke–ISCVID counts early uptake as minor; ESC can count the characteristic pattern as major

Reconcile the Two Named Definitions

**Framework-specific wording matters when interpreting postoperative metabolic imaging.** In this vignette the implantation was six weeks earlier, placing it within the early period in Duke–ISCVID.

Duke–ISCVID 2023 includes abnormal prosthetic uptake within three months as a minor imaging criterion. Its prosthetic major definition uses the qualifying uptake pattern at least three months after surgical implantation.

ESC 2023 permits intense focal or heterogeneous prosthetic or periprosthetic uptake to contribute a major criterion irrespective of the interval from surgery. That statement is not permission to classify every postoperative scan as infectious.

Interpret the Image Rather Than the Calendar Alone

**Inflammation after surgery can mimic infection, and a calendar threshold cannot eliminate that problem.** Evaluate image preparation, attenuation artifacts, surgical materials and the distribution of uptake with nuclear-imaging and cardiac expertise.

Diffuse or nonspecific activity must not be silently substituted for the intense focal or heterogeneous pattern stated in the stem. Compare with anatomy, microbiology, clinical course and previous studies.

Use TEE to assess prosthetic function and local lesions and consider cardiac CT when perivalvular extension remains uncertain. Metabolic imaging and echocardiography answer related but different questions. A positive study does not determine antibiotic susceptibility or independently decide surgery; a negative study also needs interpretation in context. State the framework and year in an examination question or clinical classification report when the definitions differ. Do not combine the favorable parts of separate frameworks into an unnamed hybrid score, and do not delay clinically needed assessment solely to reach a later postoperative date.

Duke–ISCVID counts early uptake as major; ESC restricts it to minor: This reverses the relevant distinction. The 2023 ESC approach permits qualifying prosthetic uptake as a major finding without a fixed postoperative interval, whereas the Duke–ISCVID framework retains an early-period minor designation.

Both frameworks require waiting three months before the finding can contribute: A waiting threshold can reduce confusion from postoperative inflammation, but neither named framework simply discards all early uptake. Duke–ISCVID includes early uptake as minor, while ESC uses the characteristic pattern irrespective of the surgical interval.

Both frameworks classify any postoperative FDG uptake as major: Metabolic activity can reflect healing or other noninfectious processes. Pattern, location, preparation and expert interpretation matter; the statement also overlooks the Duke–ISCVID early-implant minor category.

Duke–ISCVID diagnostic criteria, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciad271

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: During valve surgery, the surgeon documents vegetation and destructive infection. Preoperative imaging did not meet a major criterion, and subsequent histology and microbiology do not provide confirmation. What role can the operative observation have under Duke–ISCVID 2023?
options: It can provide the surgical major clinical criterion in this specified setting
It independently constitutes pathological definite IE without tissue confirmation
It contributes only a vascular minor criterion because it was observed directly
It cannot contribute unless the valve culture is positive
questions.explanation:
Direct Surgical Inspection and Pathological Confirmation

Correct answer: It can provide the surgical major clinical criterion in this specified setting

Document the Operative Anatomy Precisely

**Duke–ISCVID 2023 adds a surgical major clinical criterion for directly observed IE when qualifying imaging and subsequent pathological or microbiological confirmation are absent.** The observation should describe the lesion rather than merely record a general impression.

Examples include vegetation, abscess, tissue destruction and infected prosthetic dehiscence. Operative documentation should identify the involved structure and extent.

The specified situation matters: this is not a mechanism for multiplying the same anatomical evidence into extra major categories when it has already been established by the other routes.

Continue to Obtain Tissue Evidence

**Macroscopic evidence is not equivalent to histological confirmation.** Send appropriate specimens for microbiology, histopathology and selected molecular testing whenever feasible.

Prior antibiotics can suppress growth, while sampling and processing can affect both culture and microscopy. A negative culture does not by itself prove that the observed lesion was sterile.

Conversely, a nonspecific mass or degenerative lesion must not be relabeled as infectious simply because it was excised. Correlate operative findings with the clinical presentation, blood results and tissue assessment. One surgical major finding alone is not the same as satisfying a clinical definite combination. If qualifying pathological evidence becomes available, interpret it using that separate route rather than continuing to describe the case as supported only by surgical inspection. The purpose of recognizing operative evidence is to capture an important diagnostic observation, not to relax careful specimen collection or infer the pathogen and antimicrobial course without evidence.

It independently constitutes pathological definite IE without tissue confirmation: Qualifying tissue microbiology or active-endocarditis histology can establish the pathological route. A surgeon’s direct macroscopic observation is instead assigned a specific clinical major role when the stated other confirmation is unavailable.

It contributes only a vascular minor criterion because it was observed directly: Vascular minor evidence concerns embolic and other specified vascular manifestations. Directly observed valve destruction or vegetation is evidence at the cardiac source and belongs to the separate surgical major provision.

It cannot contribute unless the valve culture is positive: Positive tissue microbiology would be valuable and should be sought. Its absence does not automatically erase a well-documented operative finding, particularly after antibiotics; the revised surgical major provision addresses this diagnostic gap.

Duke–ISCVID diagnostic criteria, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciad271

questions.question: A patient with a prosthetic mitral valve has persistent fever and repeatedly positive cultures for a typical IE organism. TTE does not adequately visualize the sewing ring and reports no definite vegetation. Which cardiac investigation is the most appropriate next step?
options: Transesophageal echocardiography
Repeat transthoracic echocardiography as the sole next study
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging
ECG-gated cardiac CT
questions.explanation:
Prosthetic-Valve Infection After a Nondiagnostic TTE

Correct answer: Transesophageal echocardiography

Select Echocardiography for the Anatomical Question

**A nondiagnostic TTE around a prosthesis does not exclude IE.** TEE improves visualization of vegetations, prosthetic stability, regurgitation and adjacent structures.

TTE remains valuable for ventricular function, pressure estimates and the hemodynamic consequences of valve disease. The two examinations are complementary rather than mutually exclusive.

Prosthetic acoustic shadowing and difficult windows can conceal lesions. Interpret the report’s technical adequacy rather than equating no definite vegetation with a high-quality negative study.

Define Extent as Well as Presence

**The examination should assess destruction and local extension, not only measure a visible mass.** Look for abscess, pseudoaneurysm, fistula, dehiscence and important new regurgitation.

TEE is recommended when TTE is negative or inconclusive and suspicion remains high, and is particularly important with prostheses or devices. ESC 2023 generally also uses TEE after a positive TTE to assess complications; an exception is isolated right-sided native-valve disease with a good-quality conclusive TTE.

If TEE is inconclusive or cannot be performed, select additional imaging according to the unresolved question. questions.question: A clinically stable patient has persistent typical-organism bacteremia and a high clinical suspicion of IE. Initial TTE and TEE are negative, with no new shock, HF or conduction change. Which follow-up imaging plan best follows ESC 2023?
options: Replace repeat echocardiography with a negative native-valve FDG-PET study
Repeat echocardiography only at the end of the antibiotic course
Repeat echocardiography only if a new murmur becomes audible
Repeat echocardiography in approximately five to seven days while continuing the investigation
questions.explanation:
Repeat Imaging After an Initially Negative Examination

Correct answer: Repeat echocardiography in approximately five to seven days while continuing the investigation

Allow for Evolving or Initially Occult Lesions

**Early IE can be present before a vegetation or local complication becomes demonstrable.** Negative initial imaging must be interpreted against the quality of the examination and the remaining clinical probability.

ESC 2023 recommends repeating echocardiography after about five to seven days when the initial examination is normal or inconclusive and suspicion remains high.

The interval is not a required delay in a deteriorating patient. New HF, embolism, atrioventricular block or other evidence of complication warrants reassessment promptly rather than waiting for a scheduled date.

Use the Interval to Resolve the Diagnostic Problem

**Ongoing microbiology and source evaluation are part of the repeat-imaging strategy.** Document culture clearance, confirm organism identity and susceptibility, and assess devices or extracardiac foci.

The choice of repeat TTE, TEE and additional CT or nuclear imaging depends on the suspected structure and the limitations of previous studies. A prosthesis, complex implant or concern for local invasion may require a multimodal approach.

A negative first TEE is more reassuring when pretest probability is low and a credible alternative explains the illness than when typical bacteremia persists. Conversely, repeated imaging should answer a specific question rather than accumulate tests without reassessing the diagnosis. Compare with previous images for new regurgitation or dehiscence and communicate the organism and clinical changes to the imaging team. The intended clinical action is continued active investigation; it is neither untreated observation nor automatic prolonged IE therapy based solely on persistent concern. Treatment and classification are updated as the combined evidence develops.

Replace repeat echocardiography with a negative native-valve FDG-PET study: PET can add selected diagnostic or extracardiac information. Its limited native-valve sensitivity means that a negative scan cannot substitute for an appropriate repeat echocardiographic assessment.

Repeat echocardiography only at the end of the antibiotic course: End-of-treatment imaging can provide a useful reference after a diagnosed episode. It is too late to resolve persistent high diagnostic suspicion or detect an evolving lesion during the current illness.

Repeat echocardiography only if a new murmur becomes audible: A new murmur can prompt reassessment but is not a prerequisite for repeat imaging. Persistent high suspicion and bacteremia justify follow-up even before an audible valve abnormality develops.

questions.question: A patient with aortic-valve IE develops new PR prolongation. TEE suggests a periannular abnormality but cannot define its extent because of prosthetic artifact. The patient is stable enough for additional imaging. Which test best clarifies the suspected local complication?
options: FDG-PET/CT without a dedicated cardiac angiographic acquisition
Repeat TEE after a further five to seven days
ECG-gated contrast-enhanced cardiac CT
Contrast-enhanced cardiac MRI
questions.explanation:
Cardiac CT for Suspected Aortic Root Extension

Correct answer: ECG-gated contrast-enhanced cardiac CT

Connect Conduction Change With Local Anatomy

**New conduction disease during aortic IE raises concern for periannular extension.** The conduction system lies near the aortic annulus, so PR prolongation or AV block can be an anatomical warning rather than an isolated electrical problem.

An abscess is an infected periannular collection; a pseudoaneurysm has communication with the cardiovascular lumen, and a fistula connects adjacent chambers or vascular structures.

Clinical deterioration, HF or progressive conduction disease also requires urgent multidisciplinary assessment. Additional imaging must not become a reason to postpone necessary source-control decisions.

Combine CT Anatomy With Echocardiographic Function

**Cardiac CT is particularly useful for perivalvular or periprosthetic complications when TEE is inconclusive or not feasible.** An appropriate ECG-gated cardiac protocol differs from an unoptimized routine chest CT.

Assess abscess extent, pseudoaneurysm, fistula and relation to nearby structures. Review contrast risk, renal function and image quality with the team rather than ordering an anatomical test without a usable acquisition plan.

TEE generally remains better for small mobile vegetations and dynamic valve findings. A negative CT therefore cannot be interpreted as exclusion of every leaflet lesion. The modalities provide complementary information for surgical planning: echo defines function and many valve abnormalities, while CT can map invasive disease hidden by acoustic shadowing. The new conduction finding increases urgency but does not itself identify the organism or establish the exact cavity type. Correlate imaging with cultures, examination and hemodynamics and involve the Endocarditis Team early.

FDG-PET/CT without a dedicated cardiac angiographic acquisition: PET can support the presence of prosthetic infection and find distant foci. The immediate unresolved question is the detailed periannular cavity anatomy; dedicated gated contrast CT is better suited to map that anatomy for intervention.

Repeat TEE after a further five to seven days: Repeat echocardiography is appropriate for initially occult lesions when suspicion remains high. A new conduction abnormality with a suspected periannular lesion requires prompt definition of extension rather than waiting for routine interval reassessment.

Contrast-enhanced cardiac MRI: CMR can assess myocardial tissue and ventricular function in selected cases. It is less suited than gated cardiac CT to the small periannular structures and prosthetic artifact problem that must be resolved here.

questions.question: A patient with a prosthetic aortic valve implanted two years ago has ongoing clinical suspicion of PVE. TEE and cardiac CT remain inconclusive. Which additional study best complements these examinations and evaluates possible distant infection?

Another TEE as the sole additional study

questions.explanation:
Metabolic Imaging After Inconclusive Prosthetic Studies

Correct answer: Properly prepared whole-body FDG-PET/CT

Use Metabolic Evidence When Prosthetic Anatomy Is Difficult

**FDG-PET/CT can complement echocardiography and cardiac CT in suspected prosthetic infection.** It detects increased glucose metabolism associated with inflammatory activity rather than directly culturing organisms.

Appropriate preparation to suppress physiological myocardial uptake and expert interpretation improve usefulness. Technical quality, attenuation artifacts and noninfectious inflammatory activity must be considered.

The prosthesis is remote from surgery in this vignette, avoiding the specific early-period classification distinction. Even late uptake is interpreted by pattern and context rather than considering all activity infectious.

Interpret Positive and Negative Results Asymmetrically

**A characteristic positive prosthetic study can strengthen the diagnosis; a negative study does not universally exclude cardiac infection.** Performance differs between prosthetic valves, native valves, pockets and intracardiac leads.

Native-valve sensitivity is particularly limited. Similarly, an isolated generator-pocket signal does not automatically establish infection of an intracardiac lead or satisfy a major intracardiac imaging criterion.

Whole-body coverage can identify embolic, metastatic or other infection sites and sometimes a portal of entry. Brain assessment may still need MRI or CT because physiological cerebral uptake limits PET’s ability to characterize some neurological lesions. Correlate any extracardiac focus with symptoms and targeted imaging or sampling when needed. Metabolic imaging should resolve a defined uncertainty and inform treatment or source-control planning. It does not replace blood cultures, susceptibility testing or functional valve assessment, and a positive extracardiac focus should not lead to abandonment of the unresolved cardiac-source question.

Another TEE as the sole additional study: Serial TEE can reveal evolving valve lesions and reassess function. After inconclusive anatomical studies, it does not provide the additional metabolic evidence or whole-body infection survey requested in this stem.

Contrast CT limited to the abdomen and pelvis: Abdominal CT can define splenic, renal and other local complications or possible sources. A scan limited to those regions does not investigate the unresolved prosthetic metabolic signal, although targeted CT may follow a focus detected by another method.

Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement: CMR is valuable for myocardial characterization in selected cardiac disorders. It is less established for prosthetic infection and does not offer the requested prosthetic metabolic assessment with a systemic focus survey.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: A patient with confirmed IE develops focal lumbar pain, vertebral percussion tenderness and rising inflammatory markers despite improving valve hemodynamics. There is no contraindication to MRI. Which study best assesses the suspected metastatic spinal complication?
options: Repeat TEE as the only additional investigation
Plain lumbar radiographs as the definitive exclusion test
MRI of the symptomatic spine with an appropriate infection protocol
CT of the lumbar spine without further imaging if normal
questions.explanation:
Imaging a Suspected Metastatic Spinal Focus

Correct answer: MRI of the symptomatic spine with an appropriate infection protocol

Recognize a Focus That Can Sustain Infection

**New focal spinal pain during IE warrants assessment for vertebral osteomyelitis, discitis and an associated collection.** A valve response does not prove that all seeded sites are controlled.

Ask about limb weakness, sensory change, saddle symptoms and bladder or bowel dysfunction. Neurological deficits or concern for compression require urgent imaging and specialist assessment.

Examine vascular access and other painful or focal sites, review culture clearance and reconsider whether another uncontrolled focus explains the treatment course.

Choose Imaging for Marrow and Soft-Tissue Disease

**MRI can define vertebral and disc involvement and detect epidural or paravertebral extension.** Findings are integrated with the clinical and microbiological picture rather than assumed to be specific from a single signal abnormality.

Degenerative endplate change, malignancy and other inflammatory processes may mimic parts of the appearance. Contrast use and protocol are selected according to renal function, diagnostic need and local radiology expertise.

A collection, instability or neurological compromise can change the source-control plan and requires appropriate surgical or interventional input. Microbiological sampling is considered when the organism is uncertain or the response is discordant; do not assume that every back-pain episode must have a different pathogen from the bloodstream. Treatment duration and follow-up depend on the spinal complication as well as the valve infection. Conversely, finding a spinal focus does not exclude concomitant cardiac infection or remove a valve-surgery indication. Targeted imaging complements cardiac reassessment and supports a coherent plan for the entire infection.

Repeat TEE as the only additional investigation: Repeat TEE is appropriate if valve dysfunction or local progression is suspected. It does not characterize a painful spinal focus, and improving hemodynamics does not exclude metastatic infection.

Plain lumbar radiographs as the definitive exclusion test: Radiographs can show established destructive changes or another structural cause of pain. Early spondylodiscitis or an epidural collection can be missed, so normal films cannot provide the requested exclusion.

CT of the lumbar spine without further imaging if normal: CT can show bone destruction and is useful when MRI is unavailable or contraindicated. MRI better assesses early disc, marrow and epidural or paravertebral involvement in this compatible presentation.

  • D — CT of the lumbar spine without further imaging if normal: CT can show bone destruction and is useful when MRI is unavailable or contraindicated. MRI better assesses early disc, marrow and epidural or paravertebral involvement in this compatible presentation.

questions.question: A patient with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma has recurrent systemic emboli and a mitral-valve mass. There is no fever or inflammatory syndrome. Multiple adequately collected pre-antibiotic cultures and a directed fastidious-organism evaluation are negative. Which diagnosis should now be strongly considered?
options: Antibiotic-suppressed bacterial endocarditis
Malignancy-associated nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis
Lupus-associated Libman–Sacks endocarditis
Papillary fibroelastoma
questions.explanation:
A Valve Mass in a Patient With Cancer

Correct answer: Malignancy-associated nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis

Distinguish a Mass From Its Etiology

**A valve mass is not synonymous with an infected vegetation.** NBTE consists of sterile thrombotic deposits and is associated with advanced malignancy and systemic hypercoagulability.

Systemic embolization may dominate the presentation while valve dysfunction is limited. The combination of cancer and emboli should prompt consideration, but neither feature alone excludes a coexisting infection.

TEE can characterize size, mobility, attachment and associated valve damage. Echo appearance alone cannot reliably separate every sterile lesion from IE, a tumor or a degenerative strand.

Exclude Infection Before Choosing a Sterile-Lesion Pathway

**Negative cultures are meaningful only in their sampling and treatment context.** Review prior antibiotics, culture volume and timing, exposure history and appropriate testing for fastidious organisms.

Persistent fever, typical bacteremia, destructive valve change or an abscess would shift concern back toward IE. A directed negative evaluation supports NBTE here but does not create absolute certainty in every cancer patient.

Manage the underlying malignancy and assess an individualized anticoagulation strategy for NBTE after considering bleeding risk and the nature of cerebral lesions. This differs from starting anticoagulation solely to prevent septic emboli in IE. Infectious and noninfectious embolic lesions have different management implications, so do not transfer the treatment rule from one diagnosis to the other. Consider lupus or antiphospholipid disease when the clinical context suggests it, and review tumor morphology or tissue evidence if a discrete structural mass remains plausible. Reassess the working diagnosis if new microbiology or the clinical course contradicts it.

Antibiotic-suppressed bacterial endocarditis: Antibiotic exposure before sampling is a common reason for negative cultures in true IE. The stem specifies adequate pre-antibiotic sampling, making that explanation less persuasive while the malignancy-associated thrombotic phenotype is prominent.

Lupus-associated Libman–Sacks endocarditis: Sterile valve lesions can occur with lupus or antiphospholipid disease and cause emboli. No autoimmune phenotype is supplied, whereas advanced pancreatic malignancy provides a strong alternative substrate.

Papillary fibroelastoma: A valvular fibroelastoma can appear as a mobile mass and can embolize, so it remains an imaging differential. The systemic thrombotic cancer context and overall assessment make NBTE the stronger unifying consideration; morphology and tissue evidence can refine uncertainty.

questions.question: A patient received several days of antibiotics before referral. TEE now shows a destructive valve lesion, but all blood cultures collected after treatment are negative. Which interpretation should guide the initial culture-negative assessment?
options: The negative cultures preferentially establish a fungal cause
Negative cultures make a nonbacterial thrombotic lesion the leading explanation
Common IE bacteria may have been suppressed by prior treatment
The negative cultures justify limiting treatment to fastidious intracellular organisms
questions.explanation:
Culture Negativity After Empirical Antibiotics

Correct answer: Common IE bacteria may have been suppressed by prior treatment

Separate Two Different Culture-Negative Scenarios

**The antibiotic history is central to interpreting BCNE.** A negative specimen obtained after active treatment has a different meaning from adequately sampled untreated blood that remains negative.

Common bacterial IE may become culture negative after antibiotics. Obtain the exact agents, doses, timing and any cultures drawn before treatment, including records from the referring facility.

A second scenario involves organisms not recovered by routine methods despite no previous antibiotics. Exposure, geography, valve setting and immune status guide the additional tests in that setting.

Retain Diagnostic Breadth While Improving Etiological Evidence

**There is no single universal empirical BCNE regimen supported for every patient.** Valve type, acquisition, presentation, resistance risk, previous treatment and organ function determine the initial plan.

Coordinate infectious-disease and microbiology review, obtain appropriate current cultures and use targeted serology or molecular testing when indicated. Do not stop necessary treatment in an unstable or complicated case merely to create an antibiotic-free sampling period.

If surgery is indicated, operative material offers an opportunity for complementary culture, histology and molecular diagnosis. A negative valve culture after treatment also does not exclude infection. Review sterile mimics when the overall phenotype is inconsistent, but do not infer them solely from suppressed cultures. Once reliable organism evidence emerges, narrow the antimicrobial plan and reassess duration, toxicity and source control. Repeatedly broadening empirical antibiotics without addressing specimen timing or anatomy can produce toxicity without resolving why cultures are negative. A disciplined review distinguishes failure to recover an ordinary pathogen from a genuinely unusual infection.

The negative cultures preferentially establish a fungal cause: Fungal IE can be difficult to diagnose and requires consideration with relevant risk factors. Post-treatment culture negativity is not specific for fungi and commonly reflects suppression of ordinary bacteria.

Negative cultures make a nonbacterial thrombotic lesion the leading explanation: NBTE is an important differential when the clinical context suggests a sterile thrombotic process. Cultures collected after antibiotics lose sensitivity, so their negativity cannot by itself override a destructive infectious phenotype.

The negative cultures justify limiting treatment to fastidious intracellular organisms: Fastidious infection deserves a directed investigation, especially without prior antibiotics. Here antibiotic exposure makes suppressed staphylococci, streptococci or enterococci important; a narrow fastidious-only approach can omit plausible causes.

questions.question: A stable adult with a prosthetic valve has a compatible subacute IE syndrome. Adequate pre-antibiotic cultures remain negative after 72 hours. No organism has been identified. Which next diagnostic strategy is most appropriate?
options: Broad-range bacterial PCR on blood without serological investigation
Extended routine-culture incubation without additional organism-directed tests
Laboratory review with Coxiella/Bartonella serology and directed molecular testing
Fungal biomarkers and repeat cultures without bacterial fastidious-organism testing
questions.explanation:
Escalating an Untreated Culture-Negative Investigation

Correct answer: Laboratory review with Coxiella/Bartonella serology and directed molecular testing

Broaden Testing According to the Remaining Probability

**The AHA 2025 statement proposes expanding the investigation when cultures remain negative after approximately seventy-two hours.** This is a practical trigger for a coordinated assessment, not proof of a particular rare pathogen.

Review blood volume, previous antibiotics, identification methods and whether selected organisms require special conditions or longer incubation. Communicate directly with the laboratory about the prosthesis and clinical syndrome.

Coxiella and Bartonella serology are prominent components. Consider Brucella with relevant residence, travel or exposure and use organism-specific blood PCR or broader molecular methods when appropriate and available.

Connect Each Test With a Clinical Hypothesis

**History should include animal contact, occupational exposure, body lice, housing conditions, travel, surgery and implanted material.** These clues alter probability but do not replace confirmatory evidence.

A blood PCR can be helpful for specified organisms; a negative assay may not exclude a low-level or tissue-predominant infection. Broad-range or metagenomic tests have contamination and interpretation limitations.

Plan operative tissue handling before surgery if tissue is likely to become available. Histology can support infection, suggest particular organisms or reveal a sterile mimic, while tissue molecular testing may identify a cause after blood cultures fail. Continue cardiac and extracardiac assessment to define urgency. Do not wait for every send-away result before treating HF, an abscess or another source-control indication. The diagnostic sequence should improve the chance of targeted treatment while respecting the patient’s immediate clinical needs, rather than turning a culture-negative label into an indefinite unselected test panel.

Broad-range bacterial PCR on blood without serological investigation: Broad molecular methods can provide useful evidence in selected culture-negative cases. A negative blood assay may miss low-burden or tissue-predominant infection, so it should not replace the complementary serological and laboratory assessment.

Extended routine-culture incubation without additional organism-directed tests: Prolonged incubation can help recover selected slow-growing organisms and is worth discussing with microbiology. It does not address nonculturable causes adequately, so it is less complete than the coordinated serological and molecular evaluation.

Fungal biomarkers and repeat cultures without bacterial fastidious-organism testing: Fungal investigation is relevant with a compatible risk setting and prosthetic infection can be fungal. Restricting the evaluation to that pathway overlooks common fastidious BCNE causes that require specific serological or molecular methods.

AHA blood culture-negative endocarditis scientific statement, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1161/JAHA.124.040218

questions.question: A livestock worker with pre-existing aortic-valve disease has months of constitutional symptoms, negative routine cultures and a small valve lesion. Phase-I C. burnetii IgG is 1:3200. Which cause is most strongly supported?
options: Tropheryma whipplei endocarditis
Bartonella henselae endocarditis
Brucella endocarditis
Coxiella burnetii endocarditis
questions.explanation:
Coxiella Endocarditis With a Subtle Valve Lesion

Correct answer: Coxiella burnetii endocarditis

Interpret Phase-I Evidence in the Clinical Setting

**Persistent focal Q fever can involve a valve or vascular structure and may produce an indolent culture-negative illness.** Pre-existing valvular disease increases concern in a patient with a compatible syndrome.

Duke–ISCVID uses phase-I IgG greater than ==1:800== as a microbiological major criterion, with assay-specific equivalent interpretation where appropriate. The stated ==1:3200== result exceeds that threshold.

A serological result should be linked to a persistent focal syndrome rather than treated as a complete diagnosis in isolation. Assess cardiac anatomy and consider vascular infection where the history or imaging suggests it.

Use a Prolonged Pathogen-Specific Treatment Plan

**Coxiella IE requires a different course from routine pyogenic bacterial IE.** CDC guidance for adults recommends doxycycline ==100 mg== every twelve hours plus hydroxychloroquine ==200 mg== every eight hours for at least eighteen months.

Duration is individualized using clinical and serological response with specialist follow-up; prosthetic or difficult focal disease may need longer treatment. A short doxycycline course used for acute Q fever is not sufficient for endocarditis.

Review drug interactions and tolerability, assess relevant baseline risks and arrange retinal monitoring during hydroxychloroquine therapy. Follow serology and clinical status rather than using one titre as an automatic stop rule. Investigate persistent HF, valve destruction or uncontrolled focal disease for source-control needs; prolonged antimicrobial therapy does not remove a surgical indication. Continue follow-up for relapse. The exposure and serology make the answer defensible, while the management lesson is to distinguish acute systemic Q fever from a persistent endovascular infection requiring combination therapy and prolonged monitoring.

Tropheryma whipplei endocarditis: Whipple endocarditis can be indolent and culture negative, sometimes with preceding arthralgia. It requires appropriate molecular or tissue evidence and does not explain the stated Coxiella serological pattern as well.

Bartonella henselae endocarditis: Cat or flea exposure and compatible Bartonella serology or PCR would support this cause. The supplied high phase-I Coxiella result with livestock exposure instead supports Q fever-associated infection.

Brucella endocarditis: Livestock exposure and unpasteurized dairy can also suggest Brucella, which warrants organism-specific evaluation in the appropriate epidemiology. Exposure overlap does not negate the specific high phase-I Coxiella evidence in the stem.

Correct answer: Bartonella quintana serology and appropriate blood or tissue PCR

Link the Bartonella Species With Its Exposure

Either can produce culture-negative endocarditis. A renal immune-complex presentation can coexist and may mislead evaluation toward a primary autoimmune disease.

Ask about exposures without assuming that a patient’s social circumstances independently establish infection. The history changes the testing priority; microbiological and anatomical evidence still matter.

questions.question: A middle-aged man has years of unexplained migratory arthralgia followed by weight loss, HF and a destructive aortic-valve lesion. Routine blood cultures remain negative despite adequate sampling before antibiotics. He has no diarrhea. Which additional investigation is particularly appropriate?
options: Bartonella serology without considering another fastidious organism
Targeted T. whipplei PCR, including valve tissue testing if available
Coxiella phase-II serology as the decisive endocarditis test
Repeat routine bacterial cultures as the only etiological investigation
questions.explanation:
Whipple Endocarditis Without Diarrhea

Correct answer: Targeted T. whipplei PCR, including valve tissue testing if available

Recognize a Cardiac Presentation Outside Classic Intestinal Disease

**T. whipplei endocarditis may occur without the classic malabsorptive syndrome.** Chronic arthralgia preceding valve disease is an important clue in an otherwise unexplained culture-negative presentation.

HF or important regurgitation may dominate, and fever can be less conspicuous than in ordinary bacterial IE. These features suggest a testing direction rather than provide organism confirmation.

Ask about weight loss, gastrointestinal symptoms, neurological features and previous treatment for presumed inflammatory arthritis. Reconsider the diagnosis before intensifying immune suppression in a compatible infectious presentation.

Use the Right Specimen and Interpret Negative Results Carefully

**Targeted blood PCR can provide major microbiological evidence when positive, but a negative result does not exclude Whipple endocarditis.** Valve tissue can be particularly valuable when surgery is performed.

Coordinate targeted PCR, broad-range bacterial sequencing and histopathological assessment as appropriate. Tissue staining and organism-specific methods are interpreted together rather than counting a nonspecific stain as definitive on its own.

A positive stool or saliva assay is not interchangeable with blood or cardiac-tissue evidence because carriage can occur. Likewise, no diarrhea does not justify dismissing a cardiac infection. Treatment evidence is limited and recommendations differ: ESC 2023 lists oral doxycycline ==200 mg==/day plus hydroxychloroquine ==200–600 mg==/day for at least eighteen months, with specialist drug and retinal monitoring. AHA 2025 describes an initial four-week IV phase, for example ceftriaxone ==2 g== daily, followed by at least eleven months of an appropriate oral maintenance regimen. These are distinct named approaches, not components to combine into an invented schedule. Assess CNS involvement because it changes treatment, and monitor for relapse and drug toxicity. Manage valve dysfunction and HF, including surgery when indicated. A clinical response alone does not establish durable eradication.

Bartonella serology without considering another fastidious organism: Bartonella is a valid component of a BCNE investigation and can cause systemic manifestations. The prolonged arthralgia and valve phenotype also warrant specific consideration of T. whipplei; the absence of diarrhea does not remove that possibility.

Coxiella phase-II serology as the decisive endocarditis test: Coxiella belongs in a suitable BCNE evaluation, but the endocarditis serological major definition uses phase-I evidence. A phase-II-only approach neither applies that rule correctly nor addresses the Whipple-compatible phenotype.

Repeat routine bacterial cultures as the only etiological investigation: Repeat cultures can document a newly detectable conventional pathogen and remain useful when sampling is inadequate. They are insufficient as the only strategy for suspected T. whipplei, which requires nonroutine molecular or tissue investigation.

questions.question: A patient with BCNE is undergoing indicated valve surgery. No organism has been identified. Which specimen plan best preserves the opportunity for etiological diagnosis?
options: Coordinate separate appropriate specimens for microbiology, histology and molecular testing before fixation
Place all excised tissue in formalin and request culture later if histology is inconclusive
Send only a surface swab for routine bacterial culture
Request histology only because preoperative antibiotics make every microbial test unhelpful
questions.explanation:
Preserving the Diagnostic Opportunity at Valve Surgery

Correct answer: Coordinate separate appropriate specimens for microbiology, histology and molecular testing before fixation

Plan Before the Specimen Leaves the Operating Room

**The diagnostic strategy should be agreed with surgery, microbiology and pathology in advance.** Different investigations have different handling requirements, and a specimen cannot be made culture-ready again after fixation.

Provide the clinical syndrome, previous antibiotics, exposure clues and suspected organisms. Send representative tissue or prosthetic material with correct labeling and prompt handling according to the receiving laboratory’s protocol.

Preserve an unfixed sterile portion where required for culture and molecular studies and a separate portion for histology. Do not invent a single universal transport medium for every laboratory and test.

Interpret Complementary Evidence Rather Than a Single Result

**Culture, histology and molecular methods answer different questions.** Culture may recover an organism and susceptibility information; histology assesses active inflammation and mimics; targeted or broad-range molecular methods may identify organisms after culture suppression.

Selected bacterial, fungal or mycobacterial tests and organism-specific immunohistochemistry are guided by the clinical probability and available methods. Broad-range sequencing is not immune to contamination.

A positive molecular result can persist after treatment and needs correlation with the lesion and clinical evidence. Duke–ISCVID specifically cautions against treating an isolated skin-organism PCR signal from a valve or wire, without supporting evidence, as automatic pathological definite IE. Conversely, negative tissue culture after antibiotics does not erase convincing operative or histological evidence. Review all results together and use them to refine antimicrobial therapy, duration and relapse surveillance. Surgical source control can improve the patient while also providing the best remaining diagnostic material; both benefits depend on deliberate sampling and interpretation.

Place all excised tissue in formalin and request culture later if histology is inconclusive: Formalin preserves material for histopathology and some molecular methods can use fixed tissue. It prevents recovery of viable organisms for conventional culture, so fixing every specimen unnecessarily sacrifices complementary evidence.

Send only a surface swab for routine bacterial culture: A swab may be used in some sampling situations, but actual operative tissue is more informative for the complementary investigations required here. A routine swab alone does not preserve histology or the full molecular opportunity.

Request histology only because preoperative antibiotics make every microbial test unhelpful: Previous antibiotics reduce culture yield but do not make all tissue testing futile. Molecular methods and selected stains may identify a cause, and culture can still contribute when properly handled.

questions.question: A patient has native mitral-valve IE caused by a penicillin- and ceftriaxone-susceptible oral streptococcus. There is no abscess or surgical indication, but chronic kidney disease makes an aminoglycoside unattractive. Which definitive regimen is most appropriate?
options: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours for four weeks
Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours for two weeks
Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours for six weeks
Vancomycin with exposure-guided dosing for four weeks
questions.explanation:
A Full Beta-Lactam Course for Susceptible Oral Streptococci

Correct answer: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours for four weeks

Match Duration to Organism and Valve Setting

**A susceptible oral-streptococcal infection can be treated with an appropriate beta-lactam alone.** The usual standard duration is four weeks for NVE and six weeks for PVE.

Ceftriaxone ==2 g== IV once daily is a standard adult option. Penicillin G or an appropriate amoxicillin regimen are alternatives when the susceptibility, allergy history and delivery plan support them.

Do not confuse this four-week monotherapy strategy with a selected two-week combination strategy. Shorter treatment is not obtained simply by stopping an effective single agent early.

Choose a Regimen That Fits Renal and Clinical Risk

**Avoiding an aminoglycoside can preserve efficacy while reducing nephrotoxicity in a patient who does not need the short combination pathway.** Review renal function, other nephrotoxins and the final susceptibility report.

Monitor clinical response, culture clearance and antibiotic adverse effects, including blood counts and relevant hepatic or renal tests. Ceftriaxone can cause biliary complications, cytopenias and other adverse effects despite the convenient dosing schedule.

Assess valve dysfunction, emboli and local extension throughout treatment. A susceptible isolate does not guarantee uncomplicated anatomy or remove the need for surgery if a complication develops. A stable patient may later qualify for an organized outpatient pathway, but that requires its own assessment of adherence, access and monitoring. The four-week answer assumes the uncomplicated native-valve phenotype stated in the question; prosthetic infection, less susceptible strains, another organism or metastatic infection requires a fresh regimen and duration assessment. Therapy should be targeted to the verified pathogen rather than kept broad because the original empirical regimen produced improvement.

Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours for two weeks: The two-week streptococcal approach is a selected synergistic combination regimen, not a two-week ceftriaxone monotherapy course. The renal context also argues against using an aminoglycoside merely to shorten treatment.

Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours for six weeks: A six-week beta-lactam course is standard for susceptible oral-streptococcal PVE and may be needed in some complicated settings. The supplied uncomplicated native-valve setting supports the four-week monotherapy course.

Vancomycin with exposure-guided dosing for four weeks: Vancomycin is an alternative when a suitable beta-lactam cannot be used, such as a relevant serious allergy. No such limitation is supplied, and it adds avoidable renal monitoring concerns when ceftriaxone is active and suitable.
