questions.question: A patient with aortic IE develops new high-grade AV block. Repeat imaging shows an enlarging periannular abscess. Blood cultures have become negative on active therapy. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Continue antibiotics alone because culture clearance excludes local progression
Permanent pacing followed by completion of antibiotics before considering the abscess
Urgent surgical assessment for locally uncontrolled infection with monitored pacing support as needed
Observe until a second embolic event demonstrates a surgical indication
questions.explanation:
New Atrioventricular Block During Aortic IE

Correct answer: Urgent surgical assessment for locally uncontrolled infection with monitored pacing support as needed

Interpret AV Block as a Warning of Invasive Disease

**The aortic annulus is close to the conduction system.** New PR prolongation or higher-grade AV block during IE can indicate extension beyond the valve leaflet.

An enlarging abscess, pseudoaneurysm or fistula is evidence of locally uncontrolled infection. Clearance of blood cultures does not establish anatomical resolution.

Use repeat TEE and appropriate cardiac CT to define extent when needed. Provide continuous rhythm monitoring and temporary pacing support for clinically important block while arranging definitive management.

Address the Infected Structure as Well as the Rhythm

**ESC generally recommends urgent surgery for local progression, commonly within three to five days and sooner if physiology requires.** The specific operative plan depends on the infected valve and root anatomy.

Some small, controlled lesions without another indication can be managed conservatively under close specialist surveillance. That exception does not describe an enlarging abscess with new high-grade block.

Involve cardiac surgery, imaging, infection and electrophysiology expertise. Device timing and pacing method should account for active infection rather than automatically implanting permanent material before source assessment. Continue active pathogen-directed therapy and review metastatic foci and organ function. A pacemaker corrects conduction failure but cannot reverse tissue destruction, while antibiotics alone may not sterilize a mature invasive cavity. The best plan therefore coordinates rhythm safety with timely source control instead of treating the electrical manifestation as a separate completed problem.

Continue antibiotics alone because culture clearance excludes local progression: Cultures can clear while an abscess enlarges. Anatomical progression is a separate form of uncontrolled infection and must not be dismissed because circulating organisms are no longer recovered.

Permanent pacing followed by completion of antibiotics before considering the abscess: Pacing can treat dangerous bradycardia but does not drain or remove periannular infection. Deferring source-control assessment because the rhythm is supported leaves the destructive process untreated.

Observe until a second embolic event demonstrates a surgical indication: Recurrent embolism is one reason for intervention, but it is not required here. New conduction disease and an enlarging abscess already identify a serious local complication.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: A patient with left-sided IE remains bacteremic after more than a week of active, correctly delivered antibiotics. Infected lines have been removed and directed assessment finds no extracardiac abscess or other continuing bloodstream source. Which next management priority is most appropriate?
options: Urgent Endocarditis Team and surgical assessment for persistent uncontrolled infection
Continue the same regimen to the planned end date before reassessing source control
Diagnose drug fever and stop infection investigations
Add an antifungal solely because cultures remain positive
questions.explanation:
Persistent Infection After an Adequate Treatment Week

Correct answer: Urgent Endocarditis Team and surgical assessment for persistent uncontrolled infection

Confirm That Persistence Is Real and Treatment Is Adequate

**Persistent infection is an operative concern when bacteremia or sepsis continues despite appropriate therapy and other sources are excluded.** An exact day count is less important than recognizing a patient who is failing to achieve source control.

Verify organism identity, susceptibility, doses, administration and relevant concentrations. Check intravascular lines, implanted material and splenic, spinal, cerebral or renal foci as indicated.

ESC describes persistence after approximately a treatment week, while cultures remaining positive at forty-eight to seventy-two hours already warrant intensified assessment. The earlier warning does not require waiting a week before investigating.

Integrate Microbiological and Anatomical Failure

**Surgery can be needed because antibiotics cannot eradicate the infected structure.** Repeat imaging assesses abscess, increasing vegetation, prosthetic instability and new valve dysfunction.

Persistent sepsis or shock may accelerate intervention when surgery is nonfutile. Continue active therapy and resuscitation while the team assesses timing and reconstructive needs.

Do not confuse fever alone with bacteremic persistence: drug reactions, embolic inflammation and other causes can produce temperature without continuing viable bloodstream infection. Conversely, a patient whose inflammatory markers improve but cultures remain positive has not demonstrated clearance. The stem deliberately removes common alternative sources and verifies effective treatment, making cardiac source-control assessment the next priority. A different susceptibility or an undrained extracardiac collection would alter the immediate plan, but neither justifies passively waiting in the supplied scenario. Document the rationale and reassess as microbiology and anatomy evolve.

Continue the same regimen to the planned end date before reassessing source control: An adequate antibiotic course is important, but persistent bacteremia despite verified therapy demands action before its scheduled completion. Waiting can allow further valve invasion, embolization and organ injury.

Diagnose drug fever and stop infection investigations: Drug fever can explain persistent temperature in a treated patient. It does not adequately explain repeated positive blood cultures, so microbiological persistence cannot be reassigned to that diagnosis.

Add an antifungal solely because cultures remain positive: Antifungal treatment is appropriate with evidence or a sufficiently supported fungal risk scenario. Persistence of an identified bacterial bloodstream infection calls for drug, anatomy and source review rather than automatic fungal escalation.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: A low-operative-risk patient with mitral IE has a highly mobile 14 mm vegetation and another systemic embolus despite appropriate antibiotics. There is no intracranial hemorrhage or other contraindicating neurological injury. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Start therapeutic anticoagulation as the principal treatment for the vegetation
Urgent surgical assessment to reduce further embolic risk
Wait for the vegetation to exceed 20 mm before surgical review
Defer surgery until regurgitation causes NYHA class IV HF
questions.explanation:
Vegetation Size Together With Recurrent Embolism

Correct answer: Urgent surgical assessment to reduce further embolic risk

Use Size as Part of an Embolic-Risk Assessment

**A mobile left-sided vegetation with embolism despite appropriate treatment is a high-risk combination.** The decision incorporates size, mobility, location, organism, previous emboli and response to therapy.

ESC uses a vegetation threshold around ==10 mm== in several left-sided embolic-prevention recommendations, but the strength and context differ. A recurrent embolic event is more compelling than an isolated measurement without other features.

Evaluate neurological lesions before intervention and discuss operative risk and the likely benefit of preventing another embolus. Early effective antibiotics reduce risk but do not eliminate it immediately.

Distinguish Strong Indications From Optional Early Intervention

**A vegetation measurement is not a universal automatic surgery rule.** A low-risk patient with an isolated lesion of at least ==10 mm== and no embolism or severe dysfunction can fall into a more discretionary discussion.

By contrast, recurrent embolism with a persistent mobile lesion supports urgent review. HF or local invasion may independently strengthen the indication or change the timing.

Do not use anticoagulation as a substitute for treating the infection and its source. Review any pre-existing anticoagulation separately according to valve type, bleeding risk and neurological findings. Compare serial imaging carefully because technique can influence measured dimensions. The purpose is to integrate anatomy with actual clinical events rather than select surgery from a number alone or wait for another indication to become catastrophic. A shared Endocarditis Team decision should specify what risk is being reduced and why the proposed timing fits the patient’s current state.

Start therapeutic anticoagulation as the principal treatment for the vegetation: Anticoagulation is appropriate for separate established indications in selected patients. It is not proven treatment to prevent septic vegetation embolization and can increase bleeding concerns, particularly with cerebral complications.

Wait for the vegetation to exceed 20 mm before surgical review: Vegetation thresholds are context dependent, and recurrent embolism with a mobile left-sided lesion already changes the risk assessment. A larger arbitrary threshold should not postpone review of the existing indication.

Defer surgery until regurgitation causes NYHA class IV HF: HF is an important surgical indication but is not the only one. Prevention of further embolization and control of infection can justify intervention before catastrophic hemodynamic deterioration.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: Which conclusion most accurately reflects the EASE randomized trial of early surgery for selected left-sided IE with severe valve disease and large vegetations?
options: Early surgery reduced the early composite outcome chiefly by preventing systemic embolic events
Early surgery established a definite isolated six-month mortality reduction
The benefit was established chiefly in prosthetic-valve infection
The benefit was established chiefly in patients already in cardiogenic shock
questions.explanation:
What the EASE Trial Established

Correct answer: Early surgery reduced the early composite outcome chiefly by preventing systemic embolic events

Identify the Population and the Tested Strategy

**EASE studied early surgery versus conventional management in selected left-sided IE.** It was not a trial of every valve infection or every patient with a visible vegetation.

Seventy-six participants were randomized, and the early group underwent surgery within forty-eight hours. Conventional management did not mean that surgery was prohibited; many patients in that group ultimately underwent an operation.

The trial’s applicability depends on the patient’s anatomy, embolic risk, operative risk and other complications. A high-risk frail prosthetic case cannot be assumed to have the same benefit–risk balance as a selected trial participant.

Interpret the Composite and Its Driver

**The primary composite of in-hospital death or an embolic event within six weeks was lower with early surgery, mainly through fewer systemic emboli.** It occurred in approximately ==3%== versus ==23%== in the original report.

The absence of a statistically established isolated mortality advantage does not erase a clinically useful embolic benefit. Conversely, a positive composite should not be relabeled as proof of every component separately.

Integrate the evidence with current indications: HF, uncontrolled infection and prevention of embolism. A selected low-risk patient with a large mobile vegetation may benefit from early intervention, while neurological injury, limited recoverability or a different infection phenotype can change timing. Continue appropriate antimicrobial therapy regardless of operative timing. The examination lesson is both clinical and methodological: know who was studied, distinguish early strategy from mandatory surgery for all lesions, and identify which outcome drove the result. This avoids extrapolating a small randomized trial into a universal rule unsupported by its design.

Early surgery established a definite isolated six-month mortality reduction: The study did not demonstrate a significant isolated six-month mortality difference. The principal benefit was in the composite driven by reduced embolic events, so the mortality claim overstates the result.

The benefit was established chiefly in prosthetic-valve infection: Prosthetic infection is an important surgical setting, but it was not the population establishing this trial’s result. EASE studied selected left-sided native-valve disease, so its findings cannot be reassigned to a prosthetic cohort.

The benefit was established chiefly in patients already in cardiogenic shock: Emergency surgery is appropriate for nonfutile IE-related shock, but that indication is not what this selected early-surgery trial established. Its embolic-prevention result should not be represented as a randomized shock-rescue trial.

EASE randomized trial of early surgery, 2012 — https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1112843

questions.question: A patient with IE has a small embolic ischemic stroke with mild weakness. CT and MRI exclude intracranial hemorrhage, consciousness is preserved and meaningful neurological recovery is expected. A periannular abscess creates an urgent cardiac surgical indication. Which timing approach is most appropriate?
options: Delay the operation until the infarct is no longer visible
Delay the indicated operation for four weeks to reduce conversion risk
Proceed with indicated urgent surgery after multidisciplinary neurological assessment
Complete antimicrobial therapy before reassessing the surgical indication
questions.explanation:
Indicated Valve Surgery After Ischemic Stroke

Correct answer: Proceed with indicated urgent surgery after multidisciplinary neurological assessment

Separate Ischemia From Hemorrhage and Severe Neurological Injury

**An ischemic stroke does not create a uniform waiting period for IE surgery.** Determine infarct burden, consciousness, hemorrhage and likely functional prognosis.

ESC supports surgery without avoidable delay for a continuing indication such as HF, uncontrolled infection, abscess or high embolic risk when coma is absent and cerebral hemorrhage has been excluded.

A TIA generally does not require delaying an indicated operation. A large infarction with poor neurological status is a different decision from the small lesion and preserved consciousness stated here.

Balance Two Active Risks

**The neurological risk of bypass must be weighed against the cardiac and infectious risk of waiting.** A periannular abscess can progress while a fixed calendar delay is observed.

Involve neurology and the Endocarditis Team and review whether vascular imaging is needed for a suspected infective aneurysm. Repeat imaging is selected according to changes and the operative plan.

Discuss the possibility of hemorrhagic conversion and the uncertainty of individual risk prediction. The evidence for exact timing after neurological events is largely observational, not a definitive randomized schedule. Continue active antibiotics and monitor for recurrent emboli, worsening valve function and conduction disease. The appropriate response is neither automatic immediate surgery for every stroke nor automatic month-long deferral; it is a timely operation when the supplied urgent indication outweighs the assessed neurological risk. Document the imaging exclusions and prognosis supporting that decision so the reasoning is clear across specialties.

Delay the operation until the infarct is no longer visible: Imaging abnormalities can persist after clinical stabilization and do not need to disappear before indicated surgery. The decision weighs hemorrhage, neurological prognosis and the risk of leaving the cardiac infection uncontrolled.

Delay the indicated operation for four weeks to reduce conversion risk: A delay may be appropriate with severe neurological injury or hemorrhagic risk in an individual case. The supplied small nonhemorrhagic stroke does not justify that fixed delay when an urgent abscess indication is present.

Complete antimicrobial therapy before reassessing the surgical indication: Completing treatment before later valve intervention can suit a stable patient without a continuing urgent indication. The periannular abscess in this case requires timely source-control assessment despite the recent small ischemic stroke.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

Indicated Valve Surgery After Ischemic Stroke

Correct answer: C — Proceed with indicated urgent surgery after multidisciplinary neurological assessment

Separate Ischemia From Hemorrhage and Severe Neurological Injury

  • An ischemic stroke does not create a uniform waiting period for IE surgery. Determine infarct burden, consciousness, hemorrhage and likely functional prognosis.
    • ESC supports surgery without avoidable delay for a continuing indication such as HF, uncontrolled infection, abscess or high embolic risk when coma is absent and cerebral hemorrhage has been excluded.
    • A TIA generally does not require delaying an indicated operation. A large infarction with poor neurological status is a different decision from the small lesion and preserved consciousness stated here.

Balance Two Active Risks

  • The neurological risk of bypass must be weighed against the cardiac and infectious risk of waiting. A periannular abscess can progress while a fixed calendar delay is observed.
    • Involve neurology and the Endocarditis Team and review whether vascular imaging is needed for a suspected infective aneurysm. Repeat imaging is selected according to changes and the operative plan.
    • Discuss the possibility of hemorrhagic conversion and the uncertainty of individual risk prediction. The evidence for exact timing after neurological events is largely observational, not a definitive randomized schedule. Continue active antibiotics and monitor for recurrent emboli, worsening valve function and conduction disease. The appropriate response is neither automatic immediate surgery for every stroke nor automatic month-long deferral; it is a timely operation when the supplied urgent indication outweighs the assessed neurological risk. Document the imaging exclusions and prognosis supporting that decision so the reasoning is clear across specialties.

Other Options

  • A — Delay the operation until the infarct is no longer visible: Imaging abnormalities can persist after clinical stabilization and do not need to disappear before indicated surgery. The decision weighs hemorrhage, neurological prognosis and the risk of leaving the cardiac infection uncontrolled.
  • B — Delay the indicated operation for four weeks to reduce conversion risk: A delay may be appropriate with severe neurological injury or hemorrhagic risk in an individual case. The supplied small nonhemorrhagic stroke does not justify that fixed delay when an urgent abscess indication is present.
  • D — Complete antimicrobial therapy before reassessing the surgical indication: Completing treatment before later valve intervention can suit a stable patient without a continuing urgent indication. The periannular abscess in this case requires timely source-control assessment despite the recent small ischemic stroke.

options: Apply the same immediate timing as for a small nonhemorrhagic embolic stroke
Consider delaying beyond a month if feasible, with repeated neurological and cardiac reassessment
Plan surgery after one week based on improving neurological symptoms alone

questions.explanation:
Surgical Timing After Intracranial Hemorrhage

Correct answer: Consider delaying beyond a month if feasible, with repeated neurological and cardiac reassessment

Use Delay as a Conditional Strategy

**ESC advises considering a delay of more than one month after intracranial hemorrhage when possible.** The qualification when possible is essential because uncontrolled cardiac disease may make waiting more dangerous.

Assess the bleed’s mechanism, volume, evolution, neurological status and likely functional outcome. Evaluate whether an infectious aneurysm or another treatable vascular lesion is responsible.

When surgery is deferred, repeat CT or MRI after approximately one to two weeks, or earlier with deterioration, can help reassess stability and timing. Continue clinical review rather than treating an initial image as permanent evidence.

Reconsider Timing When the Balance Changes

**Selected patients with unstable HF, uncontrolled infection or high embolic risk may need earlier surgery.** This requires neurological and cardiac expertise and an explicit assessment of meaningful recovery.

Retrospective series support earlier operations in some circumstances, but they do not establish a universally safe early interval. Evidence is limited and subject to selection bias.

Discuss the risks of hemorrhage expansion or conversion alongside the risk of delaying source control. Manage blood pressure, antithrombotic exposure and the underlying neurological cause according to the individual episode. An endovascular aneurysm procedure may alter the sequencing options. Neither the calendar nor a single bleed-volume threshold should substitute for multidisciplinary judgment. The stem supplies stability and no uncontrolled sepsis, making a conditional delay with active reassessment appropriate; a shock state or rapidly invasive infection would require a different urgency discussion.

Apply the same immediate timing as for a small nonhemorrhagic embolic stroke: Intracranial bleeding changes the risk of bypass-associated anticoagulation and perioperative deterioration. A stable patient with hemorrhage requires a different timing assessment from the selected nonhemorrhagic stroke scenario.

Plan surgery after one week based on improving neurological symptoms alone: Selected patients need an early operation when cardiac or infectious instability makes delay unsafe. In a stable patient, symptom improvement alone does not establish hemorrhage stability or justify bypass without imaging-based reassessment.

Wait a fixed month without repeat imaging even if HF or sepsis develops: A possible delay applies only while the patient’s risks permit it. New HF, uncontrolled infection or deterioration can require earlier intervention after individualized multidisciplinary review.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: A patient with IE develops a severe new headache and subarachnoid hemorrhage. Initial CTA is unrevealing, but suspicion of an infective intracranial aneurysm remains high. Which next vascular investigation is most appropriate?
options: Repeat noncontrast brain CT in forty-eight hours
Repeat CTA after a week of antibiotics
Obtain MRA and end the investigation if it is negative
Catheter cerebral angiography with neurovascular specialist involvement
questions.explanation:
A Suspected Infective Intracranial Aneurysm

Correct answer: Catheter cerebral angiography with neurovascular specialist involvement

Investigate the Vascular Cause of Hemorrhage

**Infective intracranial aneurysms arise from infection-related arterial wall injury and may rupture.** The term mycotic does not imply that the pathogen must be a fungus.

CTA or MRA can screen when suspicion exists, but catheter angiography is appropriate with acute brain hemorrhage, a detected aneurysm requiring further definition, or persistent high suspicion despite negative noninvasive imaging.

The tests differ in resolution, invasiveness and procedural planning value. Select the next study with neurology, neurosurgery or neurointerventional expertise rather than repeatedly ordering nonvascular brain imaging.

Coordinate Antimicrobial, Neurovascular and Valve Treatment

**Ruptured, enlarging or otherwise high-risk lesions may require endovascular or surgical treatment in addition to antibiotics.** Management depends on location, morphology, hemorrhage and clinical course.

Antimicrobial therapy is essential but is not a guarantee that a ruptured lesion can be safely observed. Selected unruptured lesions can be followed under specialist care with serial vascular assessment.

The aneurysm and its treatment affect the timing of valve surgery and antithrombotic decisions. Endovascular treatment can sometimes permit earlier cardiac intervention, whereas craniotomy and the associated injury can change the sequence. Do not infer that every aneurysm requires the same procedure or that an initially small lesion cannot evolve. Follow neurological status and imaging while treating the cardiac source. The specific reason for catheter angiography here is the unresolved high-probability vascular diagnosis after hemorrhage, not a recommendation for invasive angiography in every asymptomatic IE patient.

Repeat noncontrast brain CT in forty-eight hours: Interval CT is valuable for monitoring hemorrhage evolution. It does not provide the vascular detail required to define or treat a suspected infective aneurysm.

Repeat CTA after a week of antibiotics: Serial CTA can be useful in follow-up of selected known lesions. Acute subarachnoid hemorrhage with unresolved high suspicion warrants further vascular definition now rather than waiting for an interval screening study.

Obtain MRA and end the investigation if it is negative: MRA is a useful noninvasive screening alternative. After hemorrhage and a negative CTA, another negative screening study cannot safely resolve a persisting high-probability lesion in the way an appropriate catheter study can.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: A patient with left-sided IE has persistent fever and a large splenic abscess despite active antibiotics. Valve surgery is indicated but there is currently no pulmonary edema or shock. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Perform splenectomy before any valve operation regardless of hemodynamic deterioration
Treat the abscess as a sterile infarct because both can follow embolization
Complete valve surgery and defer any splenic assessment until antibiotics end
Coordinate splenic source control with valve surgery, considering splenic treatment first if cardiac stability permits
questions.explanation:
A Splenic Abscess Before Planned Valve Surgery

Correct answer: Coordinate splenic source control with valve surgery, considering splenic treatment first if cardiac stability permits

Distinguish Infarction From a Persistent Infected Focus

**A splenic embolus can cause an infarct, while secondary infection can produce an abscess.** Persistent fever, bacteremia or focal abdominal pain warrants directed imaging and reassessment.

A large abscess may require splenectomy or selected drainage rather than antibiotics alone. Choice depends on size, location, loculation, accessibility and operative risk.

Some antibiotic-responsive lesions can be managed conservatively, but that does not describe a large persistent focus despite active therapy.

Sequence Source Control According to the Immediate Threat

**Splenic treatment is often performed before valve surgery to reduce dissemination and reinfection risk, when the heart can safely wait.** The optimal sequence is individualized and evidence is limited.

Emergency cardiac deterioration can require valve intervention first or another coordinated strategy. Do not turn a preferred sequence into an unconditional prohibition on lifesaving valve surgery.

Involve infection, cardiac surgery, abdominal surgery and interventional radiology as needed. Continue active antibiotics and culture monitoring while addressing both sources. If splenectomy is performed, arrange vaccination and other postsplenectomy prevention against encapsulated organisms according to the relevant schedule. An apparent improvement in fever after one intervention does not prove that the other focus no longer requires treatment. Document which focus will be controlled first, why the delay for the other is acceptable and what deterioration would change the plan. This integrated approach is safer than treating the spleen and valve as unrelated problems.

Perform splenectomy before any valve operation regardless of hemodynamic deterioration: Splenic control is often undertaken first when feasible. That preference cannot override a life-threatening cardiac emergency; sequencing must adapt if acute valve failure develops.

Treat the abscess as a sterile infarct because both can follow embolization: A sterile infarct can often be managed conservatively while treating IE. An established large abscess with persistent fever is a different source-control problem and may sustain infection or seed a new prosthesis.

Complete valve surgery and defer any splenic assessment until antibiotics end: Valve surgery may need to precede splenic treatment in an emergency. In this stable patient, ignoring a known large infected focus until treatment completion creates an avoidable risk and fails to coordinate source control.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: A patient with proven bacterial IE develops AKI, proteinuria, dysmorphic hematuria and red-cell casts with low complement. ANCA is weakly positive. Which initial interpretation and action is most appropriate?
options: Attribute the entire syndrome to renal embolism without glomerular evaluation
Diagnose primary ANCA vasculitis and begin induction immunosuppression from the antibody alone
Consider infection-associated glomerulonephritis and prioritize infection control with renal assessment
Diagnose antibiotic interstitial nephritis solely because AKI followed treatment
questions.explanation:
Glomerular Injury During Active Endocarditis

Correct answer: Consider infection-associated glomerulonephritis and prioritize infection control with renal assessment

Recognize More Than One Renal Mechanism

**AKI in IE may reflect immune-mediated glomerular injury, embolism, hemodynamic insult or drug toxicity.** The sediment and associated findings help distinguish them, and mechanisms can coexist.

Red-cell casts and dysmorphic hematuria support glomerular bleeding. Complement consumption can accompany infection-related immune-complex disease, but neither a complement result nor ANCA alone establishes a complete diagnosis.

Quantify proteinuria, follow creatinine and urine findings, review perfusion and nephrotoxic exposure and assess obstruction or embolic anatomy when clinically indicated.

Treat the Infection While Clarifying Persistent Uncertainty

**Control of the endovascular infection is central to management.** Adjust renally cleared antibiotics and avoid preventable nephrotoxicity without compromising active treatment.

Nephrology review and kidney biopsy can be valuable with severe, atypical or persistent disease when the result would change management. Histology can differentiate competing mechanisms and inform any exceptional immune-treatment discussion.

Do not begin high-risk immunosuppression merely because an autoantibody is detected during IE. At the same time, do not assume that every persistent renal abnormality will resolve with antibiotics without investigation. Dialysis and supportive management are provided when clinically indicated, and valve source control follows the full cardiac and infectious assessment. Interpret renal recovery alongside culture clearance, hemodynamics and drug exposure. The question supplies a coherent nephritic phenotype in a patient with known infection, making infection-associated glomerulonephritis the appropriate initial working diagnosis rather than an unsupported primary autoimmune label.

Attribute the entire syndrome to renal embolism without glomerular evaluation: Renal emboli can cause pain, hematuria and ischemic injury. Dysmorphic cells, red-cell casts, proteinuria and complement consumption suggest a glomerular process that embolism alone does not explain well.

Diagnose primary ANCA vasculitis and begin induction immunosuppression from the antibody alone: ANCA-associated vasculitis can cause a nephritic AKI, and tissue may be needed when uncertainty persists. IE can generate ANCA positivity, so the antibody alone does not justify primary-vasculitis induction during documented active infection.

Diagnose antibiotic interstitial nephritis solely because AKI followed treatment: Antibiotic-associated interstitial nephritis is a real alternative and drug exposure must be reviewed. The supplied nephritic sediment and low complement favor infection-associated glomerular injury rather than a timing-only drug diagnosis.

questions.question: A patient with left-sided IE and a mobile vegetation has no AF, mechanical valve, venous thromboembolism or other anticoagulation indication. Which antithrombotic plan is most appropriate solely to prevent septic emboli?
options: Do not initiate therapeutic anticoagulation solely for IE-related embolic prevention
Start therapeutic heparin until the vegetation disappears
Start a direct oral anticoagulant after the first negative culture
Add dual antiplatelet therapy until antibiotics are completed
questions.explanation:
Anticoagulation Solely for a Vegetation

Correct answer: Do not initiate therapeutic anticoagulation solely for IE-related embolic prevention

Treat Septic Embolic Risk at Its Source

**IE itself is not an indication to start anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy.** Effective antimicrobial therapy and selected surgery address infection and the vegetation-related embolic threat.

A large mobile lesion or embolic event prompts an integrated surgical-risk assessment. It does not convert infected material into an ordinary venous thrombus for anticoagulation purposes.

Brain emboli can coexist with hemorrhagic conversion or an infective aneurysm, making a reflex antithrombotic response particularly hazardous.

Reassess Separate Indications Individually

**A pre-existing anticoagulation indication is a different question.** Mechanical valves, AF and VTE require their own benefit–risk assessment rather than automatic discontinuation or automatic continuation in every IE complication.

ESC supports continuation for an established indication when contraindications are absent. Bleeding, neurological injury, interactions and an early operation can require interruption or a change in delivery strategy under specialist care.

Heparin bridging can be considered when a reversible perioperative approach is needed, but it is not a universal instruction to anticoagulate a patient with an active intracranial bleed. Review the valve type and indication before substituting a DOAC, since mechanical valves have separate restrictions. Antiplatelet treatment for a coronary indication also needs individualized review. The stem deliberately excludes these competing indications, making the answer clear: do not initiate therapeutic antithrombotic treatment simply because a vegetation can embolize. Continue surveillance and address the cardiac source using evidence appropriate to septic embolization.

Start therapeutic heparin until the vegetation disappears: Heparin is useful for established thromboembolic indications in appropriate patients. Septic vegetation embolization is not an evidence-supported standalone indication, and cerebral bleeding risk must be considered.

Start a direct oral anticoagulant after the first negative culture: A DOAC can be appropriate for selected AF or VTE indications. Culture clearance does not establish a new anticoagulation indication for an infectious vegetation.

Add dual antiplatelet therapy until antibiotics are completed: Dual antiplatelet therapy has defined coronary and other selected uses. It is not established treatment to prevent septic emboli and introduces bleeding risk without addressing the infected source.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: A patient being treated for IE develops an acute disabling ischemic stroke. CTA shows a proximal large-vessel occlusion, and the stroke team finds potentially salvageable tissue within an eligible treatment window. Which reperfusion approach is most appropriate to assess?
options: Mechanical thrombectomy without routine IV thrombolysis
IV thrombolysis followed by thrombectomy using the usual bridging pathway
Therapeutic heparin instead of an endovascular assessment
Exclude every reperfusion procedure because the embolus may be infected
questions.explanation:
Acute Large-Vessel Stroke During IE

Correct answer: Mechanical thrombectomy without routine IV thrombolysis

Recognize the IE-Specific Thrombolysis Problem

**Systemic thrombolysis is not recommended for IE-associated stroke.** Septic arterial injury, infective aneurysm and hemorrhagic transformation can increase the risk of severe intracranial bleeding.

Do not use absence of hemorrhage on the first CT as proof that ordinary thrombolysis eligibility applies unchanged. The known endocarditis is itself relevant to the decision.

Urgently assess the occlusion, infarct burden, time course and neurological prognosis with a specialist stroke team. Continue infection management while the reperfusion decision proceeds.

Evaluate Selected Endovascular Treatment

**Mechanical thrombectomy may be considered for an appropriate large-vessel occlusion.** It is a patient-specific option rather than a guarantee of safety or benefit in all IE strokes.

Vascular imaging and procedural expertise determine feasibility. Retrieved embolic material can be sent for appropriate pathological and microbiological assessment when possible.

After the acute procedure, reassess hemorrhage, infective aneurysm concerns, the valve source and timing of cardiac surgery. Anticoagulation or antiplatelet treatment is not added reflexively because a cerebral embolus occurred; separate indications and bleeding risks govern those decisions. Evidence in IE-related thrombectomy is less extensive than in ordinary large-vessel stroke, so discuss uncertainty rather than presenting an unrestricted equivalence. The supplied eligible occlusion and salvageable tissue support urgent endovascular assessment while the IE-specific contraindication prevents automatically following the standard IV-lysis bridge.

IV thrombolysis followed by thrombectomy using the usual bridging pathway: Bridging thrombolysis is used for many eligible ordinary ischemic strokes. Known IE changes the bleeding risk, including infected vascular lesions and hemorrhagic transformation, so routine IV thrombolysis is not recommended.

Therapeutic heparin instead of an endovascular assessment: Heparin treats selected thrombotic indications but is not an established acute reperfusion treatment for an IE-related large-vessel occlusion. It can add hemorrhagic risk without promptly restoring flow.

Exclude every reperfusion procedure because the embolus may be infected: The infection makes systemic thrombolysis hazardous, but selected mechanical thrombectomy remains a potential option. A blanket rejection overlooks a possible benefit in an otherwise eligible large-vessel occlusion.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: A patient with S. aureus bacteremia has fever, pleuritic pain and hemoptysis. CT shows multiple bilateral peripheral nodules, several cavitating, and wedge-shaped pulmonary lesions. Which source best unifies the findings?
options: Right-sided IE with septic pulmonary embolization
Left-sided IE causing systemic arterial emboli through normal circulation
Bland venous thromboembolism as the complete explanation
Primary multifocal pneumonia without an endovascular source assessment
questions.explanation:
Septic Pulmonary Emboli From Tricuspid Infection

Correct answer: Right-sided IE with septic pulmonary embolization

Match the Embolic Destination to the Cardiac Side

**Right-sided vegetations can embolize into the pulmonary circulation.** Tricuspid infection and infected intracardiac leads are important sources of septic pulmonary lesions.

Patients may present with cough, pleuritic pain, dyspnea or hemoptysis rather than systemic arterial embolic symptoms. Cavitating nodules and peripheral wedge lesions support the pattern but are not independently diagnostic.

Obtain cultures and appropriate echocardiography and assess injection exposure, vascular catheters and implanted material. Adequate imaging should also consider whether left-sided disease coexists.

Treat Infection and Assess Respiratory Complications

**Septic pulmonary emboli require pathogen-directed treatment and source assessment.** They are not automatically managed as ordinary VTE with therapeutic anticoagulation.

Evaluate pleural infection, empyema, abscess and respiratory failure. Drainage or other source control may be needed for a complicated collection.

Right-sided surgery is considered with persistent bacteremia, severe valve-related right ventricular dysfunction, recurrent embolic respiratory compromise or other relevant indications. Vegetation size alone is not the entire decision. A selected uncomplicated MSSA case may qualify for a shorter beta-lactam strategy, but an empyema, metastatic focus or significant complication changes eligibility. Provide addiction treatment and practical care support where relevant. The key diagnostic distinction is the combination of an infected bloodstream, an embolic pulmonary pattern and the plausible right-sided source, rather than assuming that every cavity is primary pneumonia or every wedge lesion is a bland embolus.

Left-sided IE causing systemic arterial emboli through normal circulation: Left-sided infection commonly seeds brain, spleen and other systemic arterial territories. It does not ordinarily send emboli into pulmonary arteries without an additional unusual anatomical pathway.

Bland venous thromboembolism as the complete explanation: Bland pulmonary emboli can cause pleuritic pain and wedge infarcts. The repeated S. aureus bacteremia and multiple cavitating peripheral nodules raise concern for infected emboli and an endovascular source.

Primary multifocal pneumonia without an endovascular source assessment: Necrotizing pneumonia can cause bacteremia and cavities, so pulmonary infection remains a differential. The peripheral embolic distribution and bloodstream organism warrant assessment for right-sided valve or device infection rather than assuming an isolated airway source.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: A patient with a large tricuspid vegetation has persistent bacteremia and recurrent septic pulmonary emboli despite active antibiotics. The team judges conventional surgery to carry prohibitive risk. What is the most defensible role for percutaneous mechanical aspiration under the 2026 AHA advisory?
options: A selected expert-center source-control option alongside antibiotics, with important evidence limitations
A proven replacement for antimicrobial therapy once the vegetation is debulked
A routine first procedure for an uncomplicated right-sided vegetation
An established superior alternative to valve surgery in operable patients
questions.explanation:
Mechanical Aspiration in Refractory Right-Sided IE

Correct answer: A selected expert-center source-control option alongside antibiotics, with important evidence limitations

Understand the Goal of Debulking

**Percutaneous mechanical aspiration removes part of an infected right-sided mass under imaging guidance.** The intended benefit is source control in selected patients with persistent infection, recurrent pulmonary emboli or other high-risk features.

The 2026 AHA advisory identifies a potential role when medical therapy is inadequate or conventional surgery carries high risk. Large tricuspid or lead vegetations may be considered, but size is not a sufficient indication by itself.

Assessment requires procedural imaging, infection expertise, cardiac surgery and appropriate extraction expertise when a CIED is involved. Do not assume the same evidence applies to left-sided lesions.

Keep the Emerging Procedure Within Its Evidence Limits

**No randomized trial has established its safety or efficacy in right-sided IE.** Registry and other observational evidence is vulnerable to selection and treatment differences.

Potential complications include vascular injury, bleeding, embolization, valve damage and incomplete debulking. The procedure does not reliably repair severe structural regurgitation or remove every infected surface.

Continue active pathogen-directed therapy, clearance cultures and assessment of metastatic sites. In device infection, debulking does not automatically replace complete-system extraction. An operable patient with an established surgical indication still needs the usual surgical discussion rather than a claim that aspiration is proven better. The patient supplied has refractory infection and prohibitive operative risk, making an expert-center evaluation reasonable while the uncertainty is explained. Follow response and plan what to do if bacteremia or hemodynamic failure persists. This is a selected adjunctive source-control strategy, not a universal new standard or a substitute for the rest of IE care.

A proven replacement for antimicrobial therapy once the vegetation is debulked: Debulking can reduce infected material but does not sterilize the bloodstream, valve or metastatic foci. Active systemic treatment remains necessary.

A routine first procedure for an uncomplicated right-sided vegetation: The advisory concerns selected patients, especially with inadequate medical response or high surgical risk. It does not establish routine aspiration for every uncomplicated right-sided lesion.

An established superior alternative to valve surgery in operable patients: No randomized trial has established superior safety or efficacy over surgery. The emerging role in high-risk patients cannot be generalized to displace a feasible indicated operation.

questions.question: A patient months after pacemaker implantation has pocket tenderness, a draining sinus and visible generator erosion. Blood cultures are negative and TEE shows no lead vegetation. Which classification is most appropriate?
options: Sterile mechanical pressure erosion
Superficial incisional infection
Definite device-pocket infection
Contact dermatitis over the generator
questions.explanation:
Pocket Infection Versus Superficial Incisional Inflammation

Correct answer: Definite device-pocket infection

Recognize Clinical Evidence of Pocket Involvement

**Erosion, exposed hardware or a draining pocket sinus indicates device infection in this setting.** A negative blood culture does not exclude a localized infected device.

Superficial incisional inflammation is a different phenotype without pocket or hardware involvement. Distinguishing the two prevents both unnecessary extraction for a skin-only process and inadequate treatment of a true pocket infection.

Obtain appropriate cultures and assess systemic symptoms. Avoid relying on a superficial swab alone to define the entire episode or assuming that an uninflamed-looking lead on TEE proves all hardware is uninfected.

Plan Complete-System Management

**Definite pocket infection generally requires removal of the generator and leads with appropriate antimicrobial treatment.** Isolated generator exchange or wound closure leaves potentially infected connected material.

Assess extraction risk and arrange care with an experienced team. After removal, obtain appropriate material for microbiology and perform pocket debridement according to the procedural plan.

The duration and route of antibiotics depend on whether infection is isolated to the pocket or accompanied by bacteremia, lead infection or valve IE. Do not automatically apply a valve-IE course to every isolated pocket case, but do not use a short skin-infection course for systemic disease. Reassess whether the device is still needed before arranging reimplantation. A distant new site and evidence of infection control are preferred if replacement remains necessary. The important distinction is anatomical involvement: the supplied sinus and erosion move the case beyond superficial wound care even without a vegetation or positive blood culture.

Sterile mechanical pressure erosion: Mechanical pressure can contribute to skin injury, but exposed hardware and a communicating sinus must be managed as device infection. Negative blood cultures do not make localized pocket involvement sterile.

Superficial incisional infection: A genuinely superficial early incisional infection can be confined to skin and subcutaneous tissue without pocket communication. A sinus and generator erosion identify deeper device involvement rather than that limited process.

Contact dermatitis over the generator: Contact dermatitis can produce an itchy superficial rash from adhesives or other materials. It does not adequately explain generator exposure and a draining pocket sinus, which require an infected-system assessment.

Other Options

  • A — Sterile mechanical pressure erosion: Mechanical pressure can contribute to skin injury, but exposed hardware and a communicating sinus must be managed as device infection. Negative blood cultures do not make localized pocket involvement sterile.
  • B — Superficial incisional infection: A genuinely superficial early incisional infection can be confined to skin and subcutaneous tissue without pocket communication. A sinus and generator erosion identify deeper device involvement rather than that limited process.
  • D — Contact dermatitis over the generator: Contact dermatitis can produce an itchy superficial rash from adhesives or other materials. It does not adequately explain generator exposure and a draining pocket sinus, which require an infected-system assessment.

questions.question: A patient with a pacemaker has persistent S. aureus bacteremia and a lead vegetation. Extraction is technically feasible after specialist assessment. Which definitive strategy is most appropriate?
options: Complete generator and lead removal with active antimicrobial therapy
A prolonged antibiotic course while retaining the entire system
Remove the generator but retain the infected transvenous lead
Exchange the generator immediately into the same pocket during treatment
questions.explanation:
Source Control for Confirmed Lead Infection

Correct answer: Complete generator and lead removal with active antimicrobial therapy

Treat Infected Hardware as a Continuing Source

**Confirmed CIED lead infection requires complete-system removal when feasible.** Antibiotics can suppress bloodstream growth without reliably sterilizing an infected foreign surface.

Complete extraction includes the generator and involved connected lead material. The procedural plan depends on lead age, anatomy, vegetation burden, surgical needs and patient risk.

Use an experienced extraction service with appropriate rescue capability. A large vegetation or another valve indication can alter whether transvenous, surgical or selected adjunctive methods are used.

Continue Directed Treatment After Removal

**Extraction is source control, not the end of antimicrobial care.** Duration depends on bacteremia, organism, lead involvement, valve involvement and complications.

Follow cultures to clearance and investigate metastatic foci. Send removed material for appropriate microbiology while recognizing that contamination can complicate an isolated result.

If removal is impossible after a genuine risk assessment, discuss the limitations of prolonged or suppressive treatment and the risk of relapse. That exception does not justify retaining infected hardware simply because the patient transiently improves. Reassess device need and provide temporary rhythm support if required; do not assume that every removed system must be immediately replaced. Plan any reimplantation at a distant site after clinical and microbiological control. The best answer treats both planktonic infection and the foreign-material reservoir, rather than choosing antibiotics or extraction as mutually exclusive alternatives.

A prolonged antibiotic course while retaining the entire system: Device retention may be considered when removal is genuinely impossible or prohibitive, often with an individualized suppressive plan. It is inferior source control for confirmed lead infection when extraction is feasible.

Remove the generator but retain the infected transvenous lead: Generator removal alone does not eliminate an infected lead or its biofilm. Complete infected-system removal is the standard objective, with specialist planning for the extraction risks.

Exchange the generator immediately into the same pocket during treatment: Immediate replacement leaves the contaminated site and potentially infected leads in place. Reimplantation requires separate assessment of need, location and infection control rather than a same-pocket exchange.

questions.question: A patient with a CIED has persistent S. aureus bacteremia without another identified focus. The pocket appears normal and an initial TEE shows no vegetation. Which diagnostic plan is most appropriate?
options: Replace the generator diagnostically while leaving the leads in place
Exclude CIED infection because the pocket is clinically normal
Classify the episode as uncomplicated solely from the negative TEE
Continue CIED and valve assessment with repeat or complementary imaging and source review
questions.explanation:
A Negative Initial Lead Study Does Not End the Assessment

Correct answer: Continue CIED and valve assessment with repeat or complementary imaging and source review

Assess the Whole System and the Bloodstream Phenotype

**A negative initial TEE cannot exclude every CIED infection.** Small lesions, extracardiac lead segments and early disease may remain occult.

S. aureus bacteremia has a substantial association with endovascular infection. Review persistence, source control, vascular access and the device history even when the pocket is normal.

Repeat cultures are needed to document clearance. Do not use a falling CRP or an absence of fever as a replacement for microbiological evidence.

Use Complementary Tests to Resolve the Remaining Question

**Repeat echocardiography and selected FDG-PET/CT can add evidence when suspicion persists.** Their choice depends on the suspected structure and the limitations of previous studies.

A negative PET study also requires context and cannot universally exclude lead infection. Conversely, lead masses can be noninfectious, so an imaging abnormality must be integrated with the microbiology and clinical course.

Investigate other persistent foci such as vertebral infection or abscesses in parallel. If confirmed infection or sufficiently compelling unexplained persistent bacteremia supports extraction, the team assesses complete-system removal rather than repeatedly waiting for a visible vegetation. Extraction decisions incorporate pathogen, persistence, alternative sources and procedural risk. A single positive contaminant-type culture in an otherwise well patient is a different scenario and does not mandate removal. The stem supplies persistent S. aureus bacteremia with no alternative focus, making continued endovascular evaluation essential even after one negative image.

Replace the generator diagnostically while leaving the leads in place: A generator exchange is not a diagnostic substitute for evaluation of the bloodstream source. It can add procedural risk while retaining infected lead material if infection is present.

Exclude CIED infection because the pocket is clinically normal: Hematogenous lead or valve infection can occur without pocket inflammation. A normal pocket does not resolve unexplained persistent S. aureus bacteremia.

Classify the episode as uncomplicated solely from the negative TEE: An early or technically limited study can miss disease, and persistent bacteremia argues against an uncomplicated designation. Clearance, source assessment and relevant complications still need evaluation.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: A CIED has been completely removed for lead infection with a documented vegetation. The patient still requires a permanent device but has a safe temporary pacing bridge. Under ESC 2023, which reimplantation plan is most appropriate?
options: Use the original pocket once the first post-extraction culture is negative
Use a distant site after clinical resolution and at least two weeks of negative blood cultures
Use a distant site after seventy-two hours of negative cultures without considering the vegetation
Reimplant immediately because complete extraction removes any need to document clearance
questions.explanation:
Reimplantation After CIED Infection With Vegetations

Correct answer: Use a distant site after clinical resolution and at least two weeks of negative blood cultures

Reassess Whether Replacement Is Still Required

**The indication for a new CIED must be reviewed after extraction.** Some patients no longer need the original device type or any permanent system.

If pacing is essential, specialist temporary strategies can bridge infection treatment. The need for rhythm support is not by itself proof that immediate permanent reimplantation is the safest option.

Select a distant new implantation site and device strategy appropriate to anatomy, pacing or defibrillation needs and infection risk.

Use Vegetation Status to Interpret the Clearance Interval

**ESC 2023 recommends delaying reimplantation until infection signs resolve and cultures remain negative for the relevant interval.** The approach is as late as practical rather than an instruction to implant on the earliest permitted day.

Without vegetations or relevant residual ghosts, at least seventy-two hours of negative cultures after extraction is the usual minimum framework. With vegetations visualized, use at least two weeks of negative cultures.

Persistent metastatic infection, a valve lesion or another complication can require further delay or a modified plan. Monitor the temporary system and vascular access, which carry their own infection and mechanical risks. A documented clearance interval should be based on actual serial microbiology, not simply days since extraction. Continue the full appropriate antimicrobial course and arrange wound and device follow-up. The patient’s safe bridge in the stem allows adherence to the vegetation-specific delay while avoiding a preventable period without required pacing.

Use the original pocket once the first post-extraction culture is negative: A single negative culture is not sufficient evidence of sustained control, and the previous infected pocket is not the preferred replacement site. The documented vegetation calls for a longer clearance interval.

Use a distant site after seventy-two hours of negative cultures without considering the vegetation: The seventy-two-hour interval applies to the appropriate no-vegetation or ghost-free setting once signs resolve. The stem specifically supplies a vegetation, for which ESC recommends at least two weeks of negative cultures.

Reimplant immediately because complete extraction removes any need to document clearance: Extraction removes a source but does not prove that bacteremia or other infection has resolved. Reimplantation during active infection risks contaminating the new system.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: Which patient–procedure combination clearly warrants dental IE prophylaxis under current AHA guidance?
options: A patient with a prosthetic valve undergoing routine dental radiography
A patient with an isolated bicuspid aortic valve undergoing dental extraction
A patient with a pacemaker undergoing routine dental extraction
A patient with a prosthetic valve undergoing dental extraction
questions.explanation:
Dental Prophylaxis: Cardiac Risk and Procedure Together

Correct answer: A patient with a prosthetic valve undergoing dental extraction

Identify the High-Risk Cardiac Condition

**AHA prophylaxis is reserved for selected patients at high risk of adverse IE outcomes.** It is not prescribed for every structural heart condition or every implanted cardiac device.

Clear indications include prosthetic valves, prosthetic material used for valve repair and previous IE. Selected congenital-heart lesions and transplant-associated structural valve regurgitation also qualify.

A transcatheter valve is included in the prosthetic group. A pacemaker, uncomplicated native bicuspid valve or mitral valve prolapse alone is not equivalent to that indication.

Confirm That the Dental Procedure Is At Risk

**Qualifying dental procedures manipulate gingiva or the periapical region, or perforate oral mucosa.** Extraction supplies that procedural condition.

Routine radiographs do not. Other low-risk dental activities should not acquire antibiotic cover merely because the patient carries a prophylaxis card.

Use the recommended single-dose regimen and assess allergy history. Explain that prophylaxis reduces a selected procedural risk but does not prevent all IE, including bacteremia associated with daily oral activities or nonoral sources. Regular dental care and oral hygiene remain essential. For congenital or transplant cases, verify the exact lesion and current guidance rather than relying on the broad diagnostic label. Document both the cardiac indication and the planned procedure so the decision is reproducible. The question tests their intersection: a high-risk heart without an at-risk procedure, or an at-risk procedure without a qualifying heart condition, does not automatically meet the rule.

AHA cardiac group | Qualifying examples

Prosthesis or repair material | Prosthetic valve; valve-repair ring, chord or clip

Previous infection | Prior IE

Selected CHD | Unrepaired cyanotic CHD; repaired CHD with residual shunt or regurgitation at or adjacent to prosthetic material

Cardiac transplant | Valve regurgitation from a structurally abnormal valve

A patient with a prosthetic valve undergoing routine dental radiography: The cardiac condition is high risk, but the procedure does not involve the qualifying gingival or periapical manipulation or oral mucosal perforation. The cardiac and procedural conditions must both be satisfied.

A patient with an isolated bicuspid aortic valve undergoing dental extraction: Bicuspid disease increases IE risk but does not alone place the patient in the AHA high-risk prophylaxis group. Good oral care remains important; the broader epidemiological risk does not automatically create prophylaxis eligibility.

A patient with a pacemaker undergoing routine dental extraction: A pacemaker alone is not a cardiac indication for dental IE prophylaxis. Device-implantation prophylaxis is a separate situation and must not be transferred to later dental care.

AHA prevention of IE wallet card, current guidance — https://www.heart.org/-/media/files/health-topics/infective-endocarditis/infective-endocarditis-wallet-card.pdf

questions.explanation:
Adult Amoxicillin Dental Prophylaxis

Correct answer: Amoxicillin 2 g orally once, thirty to sixty minutes before the procedure

Use a Single Pre-Procedure Dose

**The adult oral amoxicillin prophylaxis dose is ==2 g== given thirty to sixty minutes before a qualifying dental procedure.** Confirm the cardiac indication and procedure before selecting an antibiotic.

The single-dose strategy differs from treatment of an established dental infection. A treatment course for infection and prophylaxis for IE have different objectives and should not be conflated.

If the dose was inadvertently omitted, guidance permits a dose within two hours after the procedure. That is a rescue provision rather than the planned timing when pretreatment is feasible.

Choose Alternatives by Route and Allergy Phenotype

questions.question: A patient with a prosthetic valve is scheduled for elective colonoscopy without active infection. Which statement accurately distinguishes current AHA advice from ESC 2023?
options: Both societies recommend prophylaxis for this prosthetic-valve colonoscopy
AHA does not recommend IE prophylaxis here; ESC allows consideration for selected high-risk nondental procedures

questions.explanation:
AHA and ESC Positions on Nondental Prophylaxis

Correct answer: AHA does not recommend IE prophylaxis here; ESC allows consideration for selected high-risk nondental procedures

Name the Guideline When Recommendations Differ

**AHA does not recommend IE prophylaxis for TEE, GI endoscopy, colonoscopy or cystoscopy without active infection solely on the basis of high-risk valve disease.** Separate procedural prophylaxis indications may still exist.

ESC 2023 permits considering systemic prophylaxis for selected high-risk patients undergoing invasive nondental procedures, including relevant respiratory, GI, GU, skin or musculoskeletal interventions.

The ESC recommendation is class IIb and based on limited evidence. May be considered should not be rewritten as recommended for every procedure or as proof of a randomized benefit.

Separate IE Prevention From Treating an Infected Site

**Active infection changes the assessment.** Appropriate treatment and procedure-specific infection prevention are not the same as giving a dental-style IE prophylaxis dose for a clean nondental procedure.

Consider the organism spectrum, procedure, tissue and local protocol if an infected site is being manipulated. Asepsis and control of established infection remain essential regardless of the prophylaxis position.

Explain the guideline being applied and document the rationale in an individual high-risk patient rather than silently combining recommendations. The question supplies elective colonoscopy without infection, so the AHA position is clear. It does not imply that the patient should avoid needed screening or take antibiotics for every future invasive procedure. Good oral and skin care, safe vascular access and prompt evaluation of fever remain broader preventive measures. A comparison question is defensible only when it states the societies and years; omitting those details could make opposite answers appear correct under different frameworks.

Both societies recommend prophylaxis for this prosthetic-valve colonoscopy: AHA specifically does not recommend IE prophylaxis for nondental procedures without active infection. ESC’s selected high-risk nondental recommendation is discretionary, not a universal mandate.

AHA permits consideration here; ESC advises against it: This reverses the relevant guidance difference. ESC moved to a may-be-considered position for selected high-risk settings, while AHA retains the no-routine-prophylaxis approach in the supplied scenario.

Both societies advise against prophylaxis in this nondental setting: That position reflects the AHA approach here and older more restrictive European advice. ESC 2023 instead permits consideration in selected high-risk invasive nondental procedures, so the blanket comparison misses the update.

questions.question: A patient has completed treatment for S. gallolyticus IE and is clinically improving. No recent adequate colon evaluation is documented. Which follow-up plan is most appropriate?
options: Arrange appropriate colon evaluation and structured cardiac, microbiological and prevention follow-up
Omit colon evaluation because a routine abdominal CT showed no mass
Investigate the colon only if overt lower-GI bleeding develops
End follow-up after the final antibiotic dose if fever has resolved
questions.explanation:
Follow-Up After Streptococcus gallolyticus IE

Correct answer: Arrange appropriate colon evaluation and structured cardiac, microbiological and prevention follow-up

Investigate an Organism-Associated Underlying Source

**S. gallolyticus IE warrants assessment for colorectal pathology.** Do not require GI symptoms or an obvious mass on routine imaging before arranging appropriate colon evaluation.

Review previous colonoscopy quality and findings and coordinate timing with recovery, cardiac stability and anticoagulation needs. A recent adequate evaluation can change what needs repeating.

Treating the valve infection does not remove the need to identify an underlying lesion or other source that can affect long-term care.

Establish a Post-Treatment Baseline and Relapse Plan

**Follow-up addresses valve function, recurrent infection and prevention.** Obtain an end-of-treatment clinical and echocardiographic reference and arrange subsequent review according to residual disease and risk.

ESC encourages cultures after completion, particularly early follow-up for virulent organisms. New fever or constitutional symptoms require prompt assessment and cultures before self-administered antibiotics when safely feasible.

Relapse with the same pathogen raises concern for incomplete eradication or a persistent focus; reinfection may involve a new organism or exposure. Interpretation uses timing and microbiology rather than labels alone. Explain oral hygiene, regular dental care, skin and wound care and the patient’s future prophylaxis indications. Address injection-related risks and access to care where relevant. Residual regurgitation or HF requires continued valve management even when infection is cured. The complete follow-up plan combines source investigation with cardiac recovery and early recognition of recurrence, instead of treating the final antibiotic dose as the end of all relevant care.

Related Enterococcal Update

**AHA 2026 also considers colonoscopy reasonable in E. faecalis IE, even when a primary source is identified.** This is an IE-specific source-investigation discussion and should not be expanded into a universal colonoscopy mandate for every enterococcal blood-culture result.

Omit colon evaluation because a routine abdominal CT showed no mass: CT may identify major pathology but does not replace an appropriate assessment of mucosal colorectal disease in this organism-associated setting. A negative routine scan is not sufficient reason to omit colon evaluation.

Investigate the colon only if overt lower-GI bleeding develops: Colorectal lesions associated with S. gallolyticus can be clinically silent. Waiting for bleeding misses the reason for organism-directed investigation.

End follow-up after the final antibiotic dose if fever has resolved: Defervescence is reassuring but does not address residual valve dysfunction, relapse, reinfection or the relevant portal of entry. Structured follow-up remains necessary after the antimicrobial course.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

AHA IE diagnosis, antibiotic therapy and management scientific statement, 2026 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001466
